lessons.title: Lakehouse & Medallion
lessons.body:
## Your learning goal

Design scalable Databricks Lakehouse and Data Intelligence architectures using workload-led trade-offs

## Practice case

The following organization is an illustrative training case from the supplied deck.

## Fourteen plants, four incompatible data habits

IoT sensors on plant machinery stream telemetry continuously, into per-plant historian databases
ERP data batches nightly per plant, with no global consolidation
Quality/OEE (overall equipment effectiveness) reporting is built by hand from spreadsheets, plant by plant
A small data-science team trains predictive-maintenance models on week-old ad hoc extracts
CONSEQUENCE
Global OEE reporting takes days to reconcile across plants; predictive-maintenance models are stale by the time they retrain; unplanned downtime is discovered, not predicted.
QUESTIONS TO TEST
Which workloads truly need sub-minute latency vs. next-day is fine?
What does a stale predictive-maintenance model cost in unplanned downtime?
Who owns the definition of "OEE" across 14 plants?

## One governed foundation, four workload-appropriate paths on top

Stream IoT telemetry through Lakeflow/Auto Loader into bronze; batch ERP nightly into bronze alongside it
Refine both into silver — cleaned, conformed schemas, one per plant domain
Build gold aggregates for global OEE dashboards and predictive-maintenance feature tables
Serve BI via serverless SQL warehouses (autoscaling for spiky report-refresh load); train/score ML on job clusters reading the same governed tables
Govern with Unity Catalog: per-plant domains, global read access for corporate reporting
VALUE FRAMING
Plant historians and ERP stay exactly where they are — Databricks becomes the shared refinement and serving layer, not a rip-and-replace.

## The enterprise problem before architecture discipline

Core ideas
Teams build point solutions: a warehouse for BI, a lake for ML, bespoke pipelines per team
Same raw data gets copied and re-ingested by every team that needs it
Every team sizes and pays for its own always-on compute
WHY IT MATTERS
Storage sprawl and reconciliation cost multiply with every extra copy
Governance is enforced (or not) differently in every silo
Nothing is reusable — the next workload starts from zero again

## What the Lakehouse + Data Intelligence Platform changes

Core ideas
One governed copy of data in open storage (Delta Lake / Apache Iceberg)
Workload-appropriate compute sits on top — SQL warehouses, job clusters, ML clusters, serverless
AI-native metadata (Unity Catalog + system tables) makes the estate queryable and governable, not just stored
WHY IT MATTERS
Engineering, analytics and AI stop maintaining separate copies of the same facts
Compute cost tracks actual usage per workload instead of the biggest always-on cluster
"Data Intelligence" (e.g. natural-language query via Genie) works because the metadata layer is unified

## The architecture in one picture

Data Engineering
Lakeflow · Spark · Photon
Data Warehousing / BI
SQL Warehouses · Dashboards
Data Science & ML
Notebooks · MLflow · Feature Store
Real-Time
Streaming · Model Serving
UNITY CATALOG — GOVERNANCE, ACCESS CONTROL, LINEAGE — ONE METADATA LAYER FOR EVERY ENGINE ABOVE
OPEN STORAGE — DELTA LAKE / APACHE ICEBERG
Governed tables in object storage can serve multiple engines without each team maintaining its own independent copy. Storage ownership and supported access depend on the workspace and storage configuration.
Candidates should be able to redraw this from memory: one storage layer, one governance layer, workload-specific engines on top.

## Say it in plain English before anything else

PROBLEM
Every team keeps its own copy of data and its own always-on compute
Nothing is shared, nothing is governed the same way twice
RESPONSE
One governed copy of data, in open storage
Right-sized compute per workload sits on top of it
OUTCOME
Lower duplicated cost, faster delivery, consistent governance
Trade-off: this needs real architecture discipline, not just a purchase
PRACTICE CUE
Ban unexplained acronyms. If "medallion" or "serverless" comes up, define it in one sentence before moving on.

## Two ways to anchor the idea

SIMPLE ANALOGY
Same runway, same control tower, same fuel depot — every workload lands on shared, governed infrastructure
But cargo flights, puddle-jumpers and long-haul jets still use different gates and different fuel loads
Avoid saying every workload uses the same "aircraft" (compute) — only the runway and tower (storage and governance) are shared
ARCHITECTURE IN ONE SENTENCE
A well-designed Databricks architecture keeps one governed copy of data in open storage, and matches every workload — batch, streaming, BI, ML — to the right compute
so speed and cost are never traded against trust

## Inside storage: bronze, silver, gold

BRONZE
Raw, as-landed
Minimal validation
Single source of truth
SILVER
Cleaned & conformed
Deduped, schema-enforced
Analyst / data-science ready
GOLD
Aggregated, business-ready
Domain-aligned metrics
BI & ML feature tables
NOT A REQUIREMENT — A DEFAULT WORTH DEVIATING FROM DELIBERATELY
Databricks documents medallion as a recommended best practice, not a mandate. Candidates should be able to say when a workload legitimately skips a layer — and why.

## Apply it

Use the practice case to explain one decision these topics change. Name the requirement, an alternative and the trade-off. The three questions below check your understanding. Pass at least two to unlock the next lesson; you can retry.

Source: T01-Databricks-Architecture-Lakehouse-Data-Intelligence_2.pptx, slides 5–6 and 9–18. Adapted for self-paced reading. Live demonstrations, hidden scenario facts and independent assessment material remain outside this course.

lessons.title: Compute/Storage Separation & Data Intelligence Platform
lessons.body:
## Compute and storage are architecturally separated

Core ideas
Control plane (Databricks-managed): UI, account, identity, Unity Catalog metastore management, billing
Compute plane: serverless (Databricks-managed, per-workspace boundary) or classic (runs in the customer's own VPC/subscription)
Storage is separate from compute. The storage account and operating responsibility depend on the workspace and storage configuration; serverless workspaces can use Databricks-managed default storage.
WHY IT MATTERS
This is THE architecture decision point — not a footnote
Classic vs serverless is a real trade-off: network control and per-customer isolation vs lower operational overhead and autoscaling
Getting this wrong either blocks a strict security review or burns budget on unnecessary operational overhead

## Control plane, compute plane, and where storage sits

CONTROL PLANE  ·  Databricks-managed
Web UI & account management
Identity & access, workspace management
Unity Catalog metastore management
Usage & billing
SERVERLESS COMPUTE PLANE
Databricks-managed
Per-workspace network boundary
Lower operational overhead
Autoscales per query/job
CLASSIC COMPUTE PLANE
Runs in customer VPC/subscription
Full network & firewall control
Per-customer isolation by design
Customer manages sizing
STORAGE — governed object storage, separate from compute. Account ownership depends on the workspace and storage configuration, including Databricks-managed default storage.

## Analyze it, learn from it, share it, run it

SERVE & ANALYSIS
Serverless or classic SQL warehouses for BI
Genie for natural-language query over gold tables
Model serving endpoints for real-time inference
ML & AI
Feature Store, MLflow, Model Registry, AutoML
Agent/LLM applications via Mosaic AI
Start from the decision the model changes, not the model itself
SHARING & FEDERATION
Lakehouse Federation to query external sources in place
Delta Sharing / Marketplace for governed external sharing
Federation is often transitional, not the end state
OPERATIONS & INTEGRATE
Orchestrators, identity providers, external AI services
Lakebase for operational/OLTP workloads
Jobs, monitoring, CI/CD turn a prototype into a supportable service
ALL FOUR CAPABILITY GROUPS ABOVE RUN ON THE SAME GOVERNED DATA — UNITY CATALOG OVER BRONZE/SILVER/GOLD, NOT A SEPARATE COPY PER TOOL

## Apply it

Use the practice case to explain one decision these topics change. Name the requirement, an alternative and the trade-off. The three questions below check your understanding. Pass at least two to unlock the next lesson; you can retry.

Source: T01-Databricks-Architecture-Lakehouse-Data-Intelligence_2.pptx, slides 25–31. Adapted for self-paced reading. Live demonstrations, hidden scenario facts and independent assessment material remain outside this course.

lessons.title: Workload Patterns & Architecture Trade-offs
lessons.body:
## Match the pattern to the workload — not the other way round

Workload
Latency need
Recommended pattern
Governance implication
Batch ETL / modernization
Hours to next-day
Lakeflow batch → medallion → job clusters
Standard Unity Catalog domain policies
Real-time / streaming

Same governance, tighter monitoring on lag
BI & analytics
Interactive

Row/column masking for shared dashboards
ML & GenAI

Feature Store + job/serverless compute → Mosaic AI
Model + data lineage, evaluation gates
Data sharing / federation
Near-real-time to batch
Delta Sharing or Lakehouse Federation
Contract, residency and revocation owned explicitly

## Workload-led trade-offs create the value

Core ideas
Different workloads need different things: latency, cost ceiling, governance strictness, team skill level
Medallion layering (bronze/silver/gold) is the reuse mechanism — raw ingestion happens once, every workload reads from the layer it needs
A "reference architecture" is a starting point to adapt, not a template to apply unchanged
WHY IT MATTERS
Matching pattern to workload is what turns a generic platform into a specific, defensible design
Reuse via medallion means the ingestion engineering cost is paid once, not once per consumer
This is the difference between an architect and someone who can only recite product names

## What "well-architected" actually means

Core ideas
Seven pillars: operational excellence, security/privacy/compliance, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, data & AI governance, interoperability & usability
A well-architected design explicitly trades between pillars — it does not maximize all seven at once
This is the checklist an architect uses to defend a design under challenge
WHY IT MATTERS
Gives candidates a shared vocabulary for trade-offs instead of ad hoc justification
Directly maps to the exit assessment's "defend the trade-offs" requirement
Prevents the common failure of optimizing cost while quietly breaking governance, or vice versa

## The seven pillars — the checklist an architect defends a design against

Operational
Excellence
Security &
Compliance
Reliability
Performance
Efficiency
Cost
Optimization
Data & AI
Governance
Interoperability
& Usability
A WELL-ARCHITECTED DESIGN TRADES BETWEEN THESE — IT DOES NOT MAXIMIZE ALL SEVEN
Cost Optimization vs. Performance Efficiency: serverless simplicity vs. classic-compute cost control at large steady-state scale
Security & Compliance vs. Interoperability & Usability: locked-down customer VPC vs. simpler cross-workspace sharing
Reliability vs. Cost Optimization: redundant streaming infrastructure vs. accepting next-day batch for a workload that can tolerate it

## Two concrete decisions candidates must be able to defend

Serverless vs. Classic Compute
Spiky, unpredictable load (BI dashboards, ad hoc queries)
Small platform team, low ops appetite
Security posture accepts Databricks-managed network isolation
FAVOR SERVERLESS WHEN
FAVOR CLASSIC WHEN
Strict customer-VPC / firewall requirement
Large, steady-state workload where manual sizing beats autoscaling cost
Security team requires full network control
Streaming vs. Batch Ingestion
Action must be taken within minutes of the event (fraud, safety)
Cost of being late is measurable and high
Source natively emits events (CDC, IoT, clickstream)
FAVOR STREAMING WHEN
FAVOR BATCH WHEN
Next-day freshness is genuinely acceptable to the business
Team has no streaming operational experience yet
Source only produces periodic batch extracts anyway

title: T02 · Data Ingestion, Streaming & Change Processing

lessons.title: Batch Ingestion & Auto Loader & Schema Evolution
lessons.body:
## Your learning goal

Design resilient batch, streaming and change-processing solutions with reliable incremental semantics

## Practice case

The following organization is an illustrative training case from the supplied deck.

## Six hundred stores, three ingestion shapes, and no shared discipline across any of them

Point-of-sale files land nightly from ~600 stores as CSV drops in cloud storage — schema varies by store banner since a POS vendor migration, and stores on poor connectivity post hours late
Web and app clickstream events stream continuously through Kafka into cloud storage as JSON — mobile sessions in particular arrive minutes late and out of order
The legacy on-prem Oracle order-management system exposes changes only as a transaction-log CDC feed — inserts, updates and deletes, no full re-extract option at this volume
The customer-profile dimension has always been overwrite-in-place (SCD1): marketing now wants full history for attribution modeling, and finance wants an audit trail for order status changes
Every one of the last four nightly loads has failed at least once — a schema drift, a re-run that duplicated a day of orders, or a stream that had to reprocess three days of clickstream after a bad restart

## Match the pattern to what each source actually is — not one tool for everything

POS batch files: Auto Loader with schemaEvolutionMode=addNewColumns — scales past what COPY INTO comfortably tracks across 600 stores, and turns “silent new column” into one controlled restart
Clickstream: Structured Streaming with a 30-minute watermark — tolerates the late mobile sessions Solstice actually sees without keeping state forever
Oracle CDC feed: Auto Loader in rescue mode landing every change event, append-only, into a bronze CDC table — nothing is merged or interpreted yet
A Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline with AUTO CDC turns that bronze feed into two different shapes on purpose: SCD Type 1 for order status (only the latest matters), SCD Type 2 for customer profile (history has business value)
Every stream gets its own checkpoint location in governed storage — a workspace restart now costs the current micro-batch, not a reprocess

## Two ways to load a batch, and what each one tracks for you

Core ideas
COPY INTO (SQL) loads new files matching a path into a Delta table and tracks which files it has already loaded — idempotent, safe to re-run on a schedule
A plain batch read (spark.read over a directory) re-reads whatever you point it at, with no built-in memory of what's new — you build that tracking yourself
Both are one-shot: the job runs, finishes, and the compute can shut down until the next scheduled run
WHY IT MATTERS
Batch is still the right default for anything that only lands once a day or hour and doesn't need sub-minute freshness
Reaching for a continuous streaming job everywhere adds operational cost — checkpoints, always-on compute — that a nightly COPY INTO doesn't need
Getting this choice wrong shows up as either overpaying for freshness nobody asked for, or under-delivering freshness the business actually needs

## Choosing the ingestion pattern — scale is what actually decides it

COPY INTO (SQL, batch)
PLAIN BATCH READ
AUTO LOADER (cloudFiles)
Scale
Small – moderate file counts
Whatever fits in one read
Millions of files
Tracks what's new

No — you build it yourself
Yes — state in checkpoint
Freshness
Scheduled (e.g. nightly)
Whenever the job runs
Near-real-time → batch-like

Manual
Manual
Inference + evolution modes
Best fit
Simple, stable, scheduled loads
One-off / exploratory reads
Continuous or high-volume ingest

## Incremental file discovery that scales to millions of files

Core ideas
The cloudFiles source discovers new files two ways: directory listing (lists the path each trigger — simple, no extra setup) or file notification (a cloud queue event per file — scales far further, needs cloud permissions)
Auto Loader is incremental and idempotent by construction — it tracks which files it has processed in state kept alongside the checkpoint, so a restart doesn't reprocess
It runs as a Structured Streaming source, so the same trigger and checkpoint machinery from chapter 04 applies to it directly
WHY IT MATTERS
This is what replaces “list the whole bucket every run” at scale — file notification mode is what lets thousands of nightly store drops be discovered cheaply instead of an ever-slower directory scan
Solstice's 600-store nightly drop is exactly the volume where directory listing starts to show its age
“Streaming” here doesn't mean sub-second — Trigger.AvailableNow (chapter 04) turns this into a scheduled, batch-like run

## Schema drift: what happens, and who decides

NEW FILE ARRIVES
compared against stored
schema in _schemas dir
NEW COLUMN DETECTED?
route depends on
cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode
addNewColumns (default)
Stream fails once (UnknownFieldException),
restarts with column added
addNewColumnsWithTypeWidening
Widens types (int→long) automatically,
unsupported changes → rescued

new columns → _rescued_data, no failure

fix the schema or remove files

Ignores new columns silently,
no schema change, no failure
Solstice used addNewColumns — the new POS vendor's loyalty columns surfaced as one controlled restart, not a silent gap.

## The _rescued_data column: the promise that nothing just disappears

Core ideas
Auto Loader automatically adds a _rescued_data column to every table it manages, capturing anything that doesn't fit the inferred schema: extra columns, type mismatches, case differences, empty structs
It's stored as a JSON blob plus the source file path — not dropped, not guessed at, fully recoverable later
This column exists regardless of which schemaEvolutionMode is active — rescue mode routes everything there; other modes use it only for genuine mismatches
WHY IT MATTERS
This is what turned Solstice's new-POS-vendor loyalty columns from a silent data-loss incident into a queryable JSON blob the team found the next morning
“Schema evolution worked” is not the same claim as “nothing was lost” — a team that never checks _rescued_data can have both true and false at once
It's the difference between a pipeline that fails loud and one that fails quiet — quiet failures are the ones that cost trust

lessons.title: Structured Streaming Fundamentals & Checkpoints & Recovery/Replay
lessons.body:
## A stream is an unbounded table — and Delta is both ends of it

Core ideas
Structured Streaming models a stream as a table that keeps growing — the same DataFrame API as batch, run incrementally instead of once
The default engine is micro-batch: new data is processed in small batches on a trigger, not row-by-row
Delta Lake is a first-class streaming source AND sink — readStream and writeStream both work directly against a Delta table
WHY IT MATTERS
Because Delta is both ends, bronze can be the sink of one stream and the source of the next — that's what makes multi-hop bronze → silver → gold pipelines composable instead of re-reading everything at every hop
The unbounded-table model is why the same transformations candidates already know from batch DataFrames apply here with almost no new syntax
This is the foundation chapters 05 and 06 build directly on — checkpoints and watermarks only make sense once this model is solid

## Triggers decide when; output modes decide what gets written

TRIGGERS — WHEN THE ENGINE RUNS
Default (no trigger specified): process a new micro-batch as soon as the previous one finishes
Fixed interval: process on a schedule (e.g. every 5 minutes), even if that means an empty batch
Trigger.AvailableNow: process everything currently available, then stop — the batch-like way to run a streaming query on a schedule
OUTPUT MODES — WHAT GETS WRITTEN
Append: only new rows since the last trigger — the default, and the only mode some sinks support
Update: rows that changed since the last trigger (used with aggregations)
Complete: the entire result table rewritten every trigger — only viable for small aggregated results

## The pipeline anatomy: source, engine, state, sink, checkpoint

SOURCE
Files (Auto Loader)
or Kafka topic
MICRO-BATCH ENGINE
Reads new offsets
each trigger
STATE STORE
Aggregation / dedup /
join state (if stateful)
SINK
Delta table — itself a
streaming source downstream
CHECKPOINT LOCATION  —  one per query
source offsets  ·  state schema & contents  ·  sink commits  ·  query metadata
A multi-hop pipeline chains this: bronze is the sink of one stream and the source of the next — each hop gets its own checkpoint.

## Four things live in a checkpoint location, not just “where I got to”

OFFSETS
Source offsets processed
in each micro-batch —
resume without reprocessing
COMMITS
Which micro-batches were
persisted to the sink —
backs exactly-once delivery
STATE
Operator metadata, state
schema and state-store
contents for stateful ops
METADATA
Unique query ID and
configuration, stored in
the offset log
ON RESTART
The query reads the checkpoint, finds exactly where it stopped, and resumes — no data loss, no duplication.

## One checkpoint per query — and replay is a deliberate lever, not an accident

THE RULES
Every query must have its own checkpoint location — two queries must never share or reuse one
Deleting the checkpoint, or pointing the query at a new location, forces a full reprocess from the beginning — that's a replay, and it's sometimes exactly what you want
Moving or renaming a checkpoint mid-flight has the same effect as deleting it
WHY IT MATTERS
Sharing a checkpoint between two queries is how teams get silent data corruption or duplication — not a warning, a wrong answer nobody notices for weeks
A deliberate full backfill (schema fix, corrected source data) is done by choosing a new checkpoint location on purpose, not by accident
This is exactly what Solstice's “three days of clickstream reprocessed after a bad restart” incident traces back to — a copy-pasted notebook with the checkpoint path left unchanged

## Apply it

Use the practice case to explain one decision these topics change. Name the requirement, an alternative and the trade-off. The three questions below check your understanding. Pass at least two to unlock the next lesson; you can retry.

Source: T02-Data-Ingestion-Streaming-Change-Processing.pptx, slides 18–26. Adapted for self-paced reading. Live demonstrations, hidden scenario facts and independent assessment material remain outside this course.

options.label: Silver tables are always smaller than bronze

questions.explanation: Delta as both source and sink is what lets each hop read incrementally instead of rescanning.

options.label: Databricks blocks it with a clear error before either job starts
Silent data corruption or duplication, with no immediate warning

lessons.body:
## A watermark is a deliberate trade: a little completeness for bounded state

Core ideas
withWatermark(eventTimeCol, delayThreshold) tells the engine how late data is allowed to arrive relative to the latest event time it has seen
Once the watermark passes a given window, state for that window is dropped — rows arriving after that are not guaranteed to be processed
Without a watermark on a stateful operation, state accumulates forever — unbounded memory growth, eventually an out-of-memory failure
WHY IT MATTERS
Solstice's mobile clickstream sessions genuinely arrive 10–20 minutes late on poor connections — a 30-minute watermark absorbs that pattern on purpose
This is a business decision disguised as a technical setting: too short drops real late data, too long grows state and cost for no benefit
It's the single setting most likely to be asked “why this number” in a defend-stage challenge

## Which operations are stateful — and the late-data timeline

WATERMARK
(max event time − 30 min)
MAX EVENT TIME SEEN
EVENT TIME →
state already dropped for this window — arrivals here are not guaranteed to be processed
late data still accepted
NEEDS A WATERMARK
Windowed aggregation
Stream-stream join
dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark()
DOESN'T
Simple projections / filters
Row-by-row transforms
Append-only bronze writes

## Two ways a source exposes its changes — and they are not equivalent

LOG-BASED CDC
Reads the source database's own transaction/redo log (e.g. a Debezium-style connector) — low impact on the source, since it's not being queried
Captures every change, including hard deletes, in the order they committed
This is Solstice's Oracle order-management feed — chosen specifically because the source can't absorb repeated full queries at this volume
TIMESTAMP / TRIGGER-BASED CAPTURE
Queries the source for “rows changed since X”, or relies on triggers to log changes — simpler to stand up, no log access needed
Can miss hard deletes entirely, and adds repeated query load to the source system
A reasonable choice for a lower-volume source where the source team won't grant log access

## Landing CDC in the lakehouse: a feed, not yet a table

SOURCE DATABASE
Oracle order-management
(the system of record)

Reads the transaction log
(e.g. Debezium-style)
captures insert/update/delete

Landed in cloud storage
as they're emitted
AUTO LOADER (rescue mode)
Ingests every event,
never drops a shape it
doesn't recognize
BRONZE CDC TABLE
Append-only — every change
event kept, nothing merged yet
This is a landing pattern, not a finished dimension — turning this append-only feed into an up-to-date, history-correct table is exactly what AUTO CDC does next.

## Apply it

lessons.title: SCD1/SCD2 & Auto CDC & Architecture Trade-offs
lessons.body:
## SCD Type 1 overwrites; SCD Type 2 remembers — pick on purpose

SCD TYPE 1 — OVERWRITE
Each change replaces the previous value in place — no history retained
Right when only the current value has business meaning (e.g. correcting a typo in a phone number)
Cheaper to store and simpler to query — one row per key, always
SCD TYPE 2 — VERSIONED HISTORY
Each change adds a new row with a validity window, instead of overwriting
Right when “what did we believe at time T” has business value — attribution, audit, compliance
More storage, more complex queries — that cost has to be worth it, not automatic

## The same change, stored two ways

SCD TYPE 1 — OVERWRITE
SCD TYPE 2 — VERSIONED HISTORY
cust_id
address
C-500
12 Elm St
cust_id
address
__START_AT
__END_AT

12 Elm St
Jan 3
Mar 11

Mar 11
Aug 02
C-500
9 Cedar Ct
Aug 02

One row. The move to 44 Birch Ave overwrote 12 Elm St; the move to 9 Cedar Ct overwrote that. Nothing before "now" survives.
Three rows, chained by __START_AT/__END_AT. The current row has __END_AT = null. "Where did this customer live on Apr 1?" is answerable.
STORED AS SCD TYPE 1 | 2
AUTO CDC produces both from the same change feed — KEYS identifies cust_id, SEQUENCE BY orders out-of-order change events correctly, and STORED AS SCD TYPE 1 or 2 picks which of the two tables above you get.

## AUTO CDC vs. hand-written MERGE INTO

WHAT AUTO CDC HANDLES FOR YOU
Out-of-order change events (via SEQUENCE BY) — a late-arriving update from an hour ago doesn't undo a newer one
SCD1 and SCD2 logic, including __START_AT/__END_AT chaining, from declared intent (STORED AS SCD TYPE 1 | 2), not hand-written conditionals
APPLY AS DELETE/TRUNCATE and TRACK HISTORY ON (limit which columns trigger a new SCD2 version) as declared options
WHEN YOU'D STILL HAND-WRITE MERGE
Highly custom conflict resolution that doesn't fit the KEYS/SEQUENCE BY/SCD-type shape
Upserts that aren't really CDC-shaped at all — e.g. deduplicating a batch load, not applying a change feed
A hand-rolled MERGE has to reimplement out-of-order handling and SCD logic explicitly, for every edge case, every time — that's real ongoing maintenance cost

## Batch, streaming or CDC — the decision framework, not a default

Core ideas
Freshness requirement: does the business actually need sub-minute data, or is once-a-day genuinely fine?
Source shape: does the source even expose changes (a CDC-capable log), or only full snapshots?
Cost of always-on compute vs. a scheduled job, and the team's operational complexity budget
WHY IT MATTERS
Every subtopic in this module is a tool — this chapter is where candidates prove they can pick the right one under pressure, unprompted
“Use streaming because it's more modern” is not a defensible answer in the real-world assessment
This is the framework the guided and independent practice exercises are scored against

## Four settings, four trade-offs — and each one has to be defended by name

THE SETTINGS
Watermark delay — completeness vs. state size and memory cost
Schema evolution mode — fail-loud safety vs. silently-never-changing
SCD1 vs. SCD2 — storage/query cost vs. the value of history
WHAT A STRONG DEFENSE SOUNDS LIKE
Names the specific setting, states both sides of the trade-off, and points at the evidence that tips it
“We chose a 30-minute watermark because Solstice's mobile sessions arrive late by up to ~20 minutes” — not “we used a watermark”
Checkpoint/replay strategy also belongs here — how much reprocessing a backfill costs is a cost decision, not just a mechanical one

## Two concrete decisions candidates must be able to defend

AUTO LOADER: FILE NOTIFICATION VS. DIRECTORY LISTING
A DIMENSION: SCD TYPE 1 VS. TYPE 2
File notification
Cloud queue event per file — cheap at huge scale, needs cloud permissions to set up
Directory listing
Lists the path each trigger — simpler, no extra permissions, costs more as file counts grow
SCD Type 1
Cheaper to store and query; correct when only the latest value ever matters
SCD Type 2
More storage, more complex queries; correct when "what did we believe at time T" has business value
THE DEFENSIBLE ANSWER IS NEVER "IT DEPENDS" ALONE
Name the factor that tips it — file volume for the first decision, whether history has a named consumer (attribution, audit, compliance) for the second — and say which way Solstice's numbers point.

lessons.title: Declarative Pipelines Fundamentals & Streaming Tables & Materialized Views
lessons.body:
## Your learning goal

Design declarative pipelines, orchestrate them as governed jobs, and enforce data quality candidates can defend under challenge

## Practice case

The following organization is an illustrative training case from the supplied deck.

## A pipeline nobody could safely repair, and a bug nobody caught for three weeks

Ad-impression events stream continuously from the ad-serving layer — tens of millions of events a day, arriving as an unbounded, append-only feed with no natural stopping point
Campaign metadata (budgets, flight dates, targeting) is a batch table that account managers edit directly — and cancelled campaigns get hard-deleted, not just flagged
The old pipeline was a chain of hand-scheduled notebooks with no declared dependencies — a campaign-metadata schema tweak silently broke an aggregate step three notebooks downstream, and nobody knew until finance asked why a number looked wrong
A tracking-pixel bug shipped a batch of negative impression counts into the pipeline; with no data-quality checks anywhere, it flowed straight through to finance's BI extract and sat there three weeks until a client billing dispute surfaced it
When any one step failed, the on-call engineer's only option was to re-run the entire overnight pipeline from scratch — including steps that had already succeeded — burning hours and cluster cost on every incident

## Declare the pipeline, govern the job, and actually watch the data-quality signal

Ad-impression events become a Lakeflow streaming table with expect_or_drop(impression_count >= 0) — processed exactly once, bad rows dropped and logged before they can reach anything downstream
Campaign metadata's edits and deletes are handled correctly by making campaign_performance a materialized view — it recomputes to reflect the source's current state instead of only ever appending
A Lakeflow Job with four explicit tasks — ingest, aggregate, export, notify_finance — each declaring its own depends_on, replaces the old notebook chain's implicit, undocumented ordering
The EXPORT task writes via MERGE specifically so it's safe to re-run — a prerequisite for trusting Repair Run instead of a full manual re-run on failure
The pipeline event log's Data Quality tab is checked on a standing basis — not just available, actually monitored — so a bad batch surfaces the same day, not three weeks later

## A pipeline is a set of table definitions, connected by the tables they reference

Core ideas
A Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline is a set of table definitions (streaming tables, materialized views) connected by the tables they reference — that reference graph IS the dependency graph
The pipeline resolves execution order, parallelizes independent flows, and handles retries — none of it is hand-coded
Two APIs, same model: SQL (CREATE STREAMING TABLE / CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW) or Python (@dp.table, @dp.materialized_view decorators over a DataFrame-returning function)
WHY IT MATTERS
Compare to a hand-wired notebook chain: every dependency has to be tracked, remembered, and re-verified by a human every time a table changes
Lumen's pre-Lakeflow pipeline broke exactly this way — a campaign-metadata schema tweak silently invalidated an assumption three notebooks downstream
This is the foundation the rest of the module builds on: streaming tables vs. materialized views (03), expectations (04) and jobs (05) are all declared inside this same model

## Imperative vs. declarative, side by side

IMPERATIVE — HAND-WIRED
DECLARATIVE — LAKEFLOW PIPELINES
Write task 1: read source, write bronze
Write task 2: read bronze, write silver — remember to run AFTER task 1
Write task 3: read silver, write gold — remember to run AFTER task 2
Manually re-check every dependency by hand whenever a table changes
Declare each table (bronze, silver, gold) with the query that defines it
Reference one table from another — that reference IS the dependency
Pipeline analyzes the references and builds the execution graph itself
Add a new table: the pipeline re-plans automatically, nothing hand-edited
WHAT “DECLARATIVE” ACTUALLY BUYS YOU
You declare WHAT each table is, not the order to build it in. The pipeline reads the dependency graph out of your own table references and orchestrates execution and parallelization for you.

## The question that decides it, not the one candidates usually ask first

STREAMING TABLE
MATERIALIZED VIEW
Processes each source record exactly once
Built for append-only, continuously growing sources
High throughput, low latency
Lumen's ad-impression stream: events only ever arrive, never change
Recomputes to reflect the CURRENT state of its source
Handles source updates and deletes, not just appends
Serves multiple downstream consumers efficiently
Lumen's campaign-revenue rollup: source campaign metadata is edited and deleted
THE QUESTION THAT DECIDES IT
Does the source only ever grow (streaming table), or can existing rows change or disappear (materialized view)? That single question, not table size or update frequency, is the real decision driver.

## Picking the wrong one doesn't error — it just quietly gives the wrong answer

STREAMING TABLE ON A CHANGING SOURCE
It keeps appending as if nothing happened — an edited campaign budget or a cancelled campaign's deletion is simply never reflected
No error, no warning — the table looks healthy the whole time it's silently wrong
This is exactly what campaign_performance would do if built as a streaming table instead of a materialized view
MATERIALIZED VIEW ON A PURE-APPEND SOURCE
Not wrong, just paying a cost it doesn't need to — a materialized view recomputes more than an append-only source requires
Correctness isn't the issue here; it's an unnecessary compute cost, the softer of the two mistakes
Still worth naming explicitly, since “just use a materialized view everywhere to be safe” is a common overcorrection

## Apply it

Use the practice case to explain one decision these topics change. Name the requirement, an alternative and the trade-off. The three questions below check your understanding. Pass at least two to unlock the next lesson; you can retry.

Source: T03-Lakeflow-Pipelines-Jobs-Data-Quality.pptx, slides 5–6 and 9–16. Adapted for self-paced reading. Live demonstrations, hidden scenario facts and independent assessment material remain outside this course.

lessons.title: Data Quality & Expectations & Lakeflow Jobs & Multi-Task Orchestration
lessons.body:
## Expectations are declared constraints, checked on every row, every run

Core ideas
An expectation is a boolean condition attached to a table or flow — Python @dp.expect_or_drop("valid_impressions", "impression_count >= 0") or SQL CONSTRAINT valid_impressions EXPECT (impression_count >= 0)
Every row is evaluated against every declared expectation as it's processed — this isn't a batch validation job run separately, it's inline
Multiple expectations can be declared per table, and each is tracked independently in the pipeline event log's data-quality metrics
WHY IT MATTERS
This is the mechanism that would have caught Lumen's negative-impression-count bug inline, the same run it was introduced — not three weeks later in a client billing dispute
Expectations are part of the pipeline definition, versioned with the code — not a separate, easily-forgotten validation step someone has to remember to run
They apply per-row, so a single bad record never has to fail an entire batch unless you choose that behavior — that's the next slide

## One condition, three possible responses to a violation

ROW ARRIVES
evaluated against every
declared expectation
CONDITION FAILS?
behavior set by
ON VIOLATION / decorator choice
expect() / EXPECT — warn
Row still written to target;
violation counted in metrics
expect_or_drop() — drop
Row removed before writing;
drop count logged
expect_or_fail() — fail
Pipeline stops atomically;
manual intervention required
Lumen uses expect_or_drop on impression counts — a negative count can never be legitimate, so drop it before it reaches finance.

## Choosing warn, drop, or fail — and what a violation actually costs

Core ideas
expect() / EXPECT (warn): row is still written, violation is counted — use when bad rows are informational, not harmful downstream
expect_or_drop(): row is removed before writing, drop count logged — use when a bad row is safe to silently exclude, like Lumen's negative impression counts
expect_or_fail(): the whole pipeline update stops atomically the moment a violation occurs — use only when a bad row must never reach a downstream consumer
WHY IT MATTERS
Fail is not automatically the safest choice — it stops the entire pipeline update, which has its own cost (a finance dashboard that goes stale because of one bad row)
Lumen uses expect_or_drop on impression counts specifically because a negative count can never be legitimate, and failing the whole pipeline over one bad row would be overkill
The decision is the same shape as the trade-offs candidates will defend in chapter 09: name what a bad row costs downstream before choosing

## What a Lakeflow Job actually is, and how it differs from a pipeline

Core ideas
A Lakeflow Job (formerly a “Job” or “Workflow”) orchestrates one or more tasks — notebooks, Python scripts, SQL queries, dbt, or a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline update — as a single managed unit
Each task can declare its own depends_on — that's what turns a flat task list into an execution graph, the same declared-dependency model as chapter 02's pipeline
A job can mix task types freely: Lumen's job runs a pipeline-update task (ingest) followed by SQL/notebook tasks (aggregate, export, notify_finance)
WHY IT MATTERS
This is the layer above a single Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline — a pipeline handles table-level dependency and incremental processing; a job orchestrates the broader workflow around it, including steps that aren't table definitions at all (like sending an alert)
Lumen's job is exactly this shape: one pipeline-update task feeding three downstream SQL/notification tasks, all governed by one explicit dependency graph
Job-level retries, alerting, and Repair Run (chapter 08) all operate on this task graph

## Lumen's four-task job, and the dependency each one declares

INGEST
Read source,
write streaming table
AGGREGATE
Refresh the
materialized view
EXPORT
Write the BI
extract
NOTIFY_FINANCE
Send the completion
alert
EACH TASK DECLARES ITS OWN DEPENDS_ON
export depends on aggregate; aggregate depends on ingest; notify_finance depends on export
This explicit graph is what makes Repair Run possible (chapter 08): the job knows exactly which tasks a failure at EXPORT should re-run, and which — INGEST, AGGREGATE — already succeeded and can be left alone.

## Idempotent writes are what make repair (and retries) safe

Core ideas
A task that gets re-run — by a retry, or by Repair Run — must produce the same correct result whether it's the first attempt or the third
MERGE-based writes are naturally idempotent: re-running the same MERGE against the same source state doesn't duplicate rows
A plain append is NOT automatically idempotent — re-running an append task after a partial failure can silently double-write
WHY IT MATTERS
Lumen's EXPORT task writes the BI extract via MERGE specifically because it has to survive being re-run by Repair Run without corrupting finance's numbers
This is the single most common way a repair “succeeds” technically but produces wrong data — a task re-ran, but its write wasn't safe to re-run
Idempotency isn't a job-level setting — it has to be built into each task's own write logic, task by task

## Apply it

Use the practice case to explain one decision these topics change. Name the requirement, an alternative and the trade-off. The three questions below check your understanding. Pass at least two to unlock the next lesson; you can retry.

Source: T03-Lakeflow-Pipelines-Jobs-Data-Quality.pptx, slides 17–26. Adapted for self-paced reading. Live demonstrations, hidden scenario facts and independent assessment material remain outside this course.

## Four ways a job run starts, and what each one actually fits

Core ideas
Scheduled: a cron expression decides when the job fires — predictable, calendar-driven
File Arrival: fires when a new file lands in a Unity Catalog volume or cloud storage location — event-driven ingestion without polling
Table Update: fires when a source table changes — ties a downstream job directly to upstream data changing, not a clock
Continuous: the next run starts as soon as the previous one finishes — for perpetual near-real-time chains
WHY IT MATTERS
A job's trigger and its tasks' own machinery (like a streaming table) can run on different rhythms — Lumen's ad-impression streaming table runs continuously, while the job that aggregates and exports from it fires on a nightly Scheduled trigger
Choosing File Arrival or Table Update over Scheduled trades predictability for freshness — the job fires exactly when something changed, not on a fixed clock
Getting this wrong either wastes a scheduled run on no new data, or — worse — misses a freshness requirement by waiting for a clock that ticks too slowly

lessons.title: Repair Run & Architecture Trade-offs
lessons.body:
## What Repair Run actually re-runs, and why it can't work without chapter 05's graph

Core ideas
Repair Run re-runs only the unsuccessful tasks in a job and their downstream dependents — tasks that already succeeded are left untouched
It requires the job's dependency graph to be explicit — Repair Run can only know what “downstream of the failure” means because depends_on says so
Available only for jobs with two or more tasks — a single-task job has nothing to selectively repair
WHY IT MATTERS
For Lumen, a failed EXPORT task means only EXPORT and NOTIFY_FINANCE re-run — INGEST and AGGREGATE, which already succeeded, are left alone, saving the compute and time of a full re-run
This is the direct payoff of chapter 05's explicit dependency graph — a flat, unstructured task list couldn't support this at all
Before Lakeflow Jobs, Lumen's team re-ran failed pipelines from scratch overnight — Repair Run is what ends that

## The run that failed, and exactly what the repair re-runs

RUN THAT FAILED
REPAIR RUN
INGEST
succeeded
AGGREGATE
succeeded
EXPORT
FAILED
NOTIFY
skipped (already ok)
INGEST
skipped (already ok)

re-run
NOTIFY

ONLY UNSUCCESSFUL TASKS AND THEIR DEPENDENTS RE-RUN
INGEST and AGGREGATE already succeeded and are left alone. EXPORT re-runs from the beginning — which is exactly why it must be an idempotent MERGE, not an append: a repair can re-execute a task that already wrote partial output.

## Why idempotent writes are a prerequisite, not a nice-to-have

Core ideas
A repaired task doesn't resume mid-write — it re-runs from the beginning, the same as its first attempt
If EXPORT failed after writing half its output, Repair Run re-runs EXPORT completely — an idempotent MERGE overwrites/corrects that partial output; a plain append would duplicate it
This is exactly chapter 05's idempotency point, now shown as the specific failure mode Repair Run exposes if it's ignored
WHY IT MATTERS
A team that adds Repair Run without first checking every task's write is idempotent can turn “the repair worked” into silently wrong data — no error, just duplicated or corrupted rows
This is a design review question, not just an operational one: idempotency has to be verified before Repair Run is trusted for a given job
Lumen's EXPORT task specifically was redesigned to MERGE before Repair Run was adopted — the two changes shipped together, not separately

## The decision framework, not a default

Core ideas
Does the source ever change after it lands, or does it only append? That single question decides streaming table vs. materialized view before anything else does
What does a bad row actually cost downstream if it's allowed through? That's what decides warn vs. drop vs. fail — not a blanket policy
How expensive is a full re-run vs. a partial one? That's what makes an explicit task dependency graph and idempotent writes worth building, not optional polish
WHY IT MATTERS
Every subtopic in this module is a tool — this chapter is where candidates prove they can pick the right one under pressure, unprompted
“Use materialized views because they're more correct” is not a defensible answer — streaming tables are correct too, for a different shape of source
This is the framework the guided and independent practice exercises are scored against

## Two settings, always named and justified

THE SETTINGS
Streaming table vs. materialized view — the source-shape question from chapter 03
Warn / drop / fail on an expectation — the cost-of-a-bad-row question from chapter 04
WHAT A STRONG DEFENSE SOUNDS LIKE
Names the specific setting, states both sides of the trade-off, and points at the evidence that tips it
“We used expect_or_drop on impression counts because a negative count is never legitimate, and failing the whole pipeline over one bad row would take down finance's nightly extract for nothing” — not “we used expect_or_drop”
Job-level choices (trigger type, dependency-graph shape) belong here too — they're cost/complexity decisions, not just mechanical ones

## Two concrete decisions candidates must be able to defend

STREAMING TABLE VS. MATERIALIZED VIEW
WARN VS. DROP VS. FAIL
Streaming table
Correct when the source only ever appends — pay for exactly-once, incremental processing
Materialized view
Correct when the source updates or deletes, or many consumers share one recomputed result
Warn / drop
Correct when bad rows are recoverable noise — keep the pipeline running, fix data later
Fail
Correct only when a bad row must never reach a downstream consumer, and stopping is cheaper than the alternative
THE DEFENSIBLE ANSWER NAMES THE COST OF BEING WRONG
Fail is not “the safe choice” by default — it stops the whole pipeline. Name what a bad row actually costs downstream before picking warn, drop, or fail; do the same for streaming table vs. materialized view by naming whether the source appends only or truly changes.

lessons.body:
## Your learning goal

Reason about Spark's execution model, choose SQL or PySpark on purpose, and write joins, transformations and modular code candidates can defend under challenge

## Practice case

The following organization is an illustrative training case from the supplied deck.

## The same metric, three different numbers, and nobody could say which one was right

Pinnacle is a freight brokerage — shipment scan events (pickup, transit, delivery) stream in continuously from carriers, millions of rows across the fleet, with five of roughly 400 carriers accounting for 60%+ of total volume
On-time delivery rate is the metric dispatch, sales and finance all depend on — dispatch uses it to route loads, finance uses it to bill SLA penalties, sales uses it to pitch new carriers
Twelve different notebooks each hand-copied their own version of the on-time-rate calculation — some measured against end-of-calendar-day, others against the contracted hourly delivery window — so dispatch's dashboard, finance's SLA billing report, and sales' scorecard showed three different numbers for the same week
A nightly PySpark job that joins shipment events to carrier ratings and aggregates by carrier routinely ran long and sometimes timed out — nobody had diagnosed why, they just added more cluster nodes and the problem barely improved
When the on-time definition was updated last quarter (from calendar-day to contracted-hourly-window), the change had to be found and hand-applied in twelve separate places — three notebooks were still quietly running the old definition two months later

## One versioned definition, a join and partitioning strategy that actually matches the data

on_time_rate() becomes a single, tested, version-controlled function — exposed as a SQL view for analysts and a PySpark job for the nightly batch score, imported everywhere instead of hand-copied
The nightly job broadcasts the small carrier-ratings table (~400 rows) into the join against millions of shipment-event rows, instead of paying shuffle cost on both sides for a table that fits comfortably in memory
Skew from the five mega-carriers is handled explicitly — AQE's skew-join optimization splits their oversized partitions instead of letting a handful of tasks dominate the job's total runtime
SQL and PySpark are chosen per team, not by accident — analysts who think in SQL query the same view directly; the batch job uses PySpark because it needs skew-aware partitioning logic SQL alone can't express as cleanly
A definition change now ships once, in one module, and reaches the SQL view and the PySpark job — and all five remaining callers — at the same time, the same day

## One driver plans, many executors process — and nothing runs until you ask for a result

Core ideas
The driver builds the logical plan and DAG and coordinates the job; executors process their own partitions of the data in parallel — neither substitutes for the other
Transformations (select, filter, withColumn, groupBy, join) are lazy — none of them touch data; they just extend the logical plan
An action (count, collect, write, display) is what actually triggers execution — Catalyst optimizes the accumulated logical plan into a physical plan of stages and tasks at that moment, not before
WHY IT MATTERS
Candidates who think each line of PySpark “runs” as it's written misjudge where time actually goes — and misdiagnose slowness by looking at the wrong line
Pinnacle's nightly job timeout was never a single slow transformation — it was the shuffle stage the DAG produced, invisible if you only read the code top to bottom
This is the foundation the rest of the module builds on: narrow vs. wide transformations (04), join strategy (05) and partitioning (06) are all decisions about what shape of physical plan you're asking Catalyst to build

## From logical plan to stages of tasks — and where the shuffle boundary falls

Transformations (select, filter, groupBy, join) are lazy — none of this runs until an action (count, collect, write) triggers it.

## Equivalent logic compiles to the same physical plan

SQL
PYSPARK
SELECT carrier_id,
SUM(CASE WHEN on_time
THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
/ COUNT(*) AS on_time_rate
FROM shipments
GROUP BY carrier_id
shipments
.groupBy("carrier_id")
.agg(
(F.sum(F.when(
F.col("on_time"), 1)
.otherwise(0))
/ F.count("*"))
.alias("on_time_rate"))
SAME LOGIC, SAME CATALYST-OPTIMIZED PLAN
For equivalent logic, these two queries compile to the same optimized physical plan and run at the same speed. The choice between them is about who maintains it and what the rest of the pipeline looks like — not performance.

## The defensible reasons to pick one over the other

WHEN SQL IS THE RIGHT CALL
The team thinks in SQL and the logic is naturally set-based and declarative — Pinnacle's analysts query the on_time_rate view directly, no PySpark required
The transformation is a straightforward filter/join/aggregate with no procedural branching or external library dependency
Ad hoc, exploratory querying — a SQL view is immediately queryable by anyone with warehouse access
WHEN PYSPARK IS THE RIGHT CALL
The logic needs procedural structure — loops, conditionals across multiple steps, or calling a Python library SQL can't reach (a ML scoring function, a custom skew-handling routine)
Pinnacle's nightly batch job is PySpark specifically because its skew-aware partitioning logic needs that procedural control, not because PySpark is “faster”
Testing and code review benefit from PySpark's ability to be unit-tested as ordinary Python functions, which matters once logic is shared across a job and a view (chapter 08)

## The one distinction that predicts where a job's time actually goes

Core ideas
A narrow transformation (filter, select, withColumn) reads only from a single input partition to produce a single output partition — no data has to move between executors
A wide transformation (groupBy, join, distinct, orderBy) requires a shuffle — rows have to move across the network so that related rows land on the same partition
Chaining ten narrow transformations costs about the same as chaining one — the shuffle at a wide transformation is where real query time goes, not the number of narrow steps beforehand
WHY IT MATTERS
Pinnacle's on_time_rate job chains several narrow steps (filter to valid scans, select relevant columns, withColumn to compute a delivery delta) before the wide groupBy by carrier — the narrow steps were never the bottleneck
Candidates who add “optimizations” to narrow steps while ignoring the shuffle boundary are optimizing the part of the job that was already nearly free
This distinction is what chapter 05 (joins) and chapter 06 (partitioning) both build on — a join and a groupBy are both wide transformations, and both pay shuffle cost by the same mechanism

Core ideas
A broadcast join copies the smaller table whole to every executor — the large side never has to shuffle at all
A shuffle (sort-merge) join repartitions both sides by the join key across the network before matching rows — necessary and correct when neither side is small enough to broadcast
Spark's Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) can convert a planned shuffle join into a broadcast join automatically, once it sees a table's actual — not estimated — size mid-query
WHY IT MATTERS
Pinnacle's carrier-ratings table is ~400 rows — broadcasting it into the join against millions of shipment rows removes a shuffle that was never necessary
Before this fix, both sides were being shuffled by default — Pinnacle's nightly job was paying full shuffle cost on millions of rows to join against a table that fits comfortably in memory
AQE is a safety net, not a substitute for understanding the decision — candidates should be able to reason about broadcast vs. shuffle even when AQE isn't available or its estimate is wrong

## repartition() and coalesce() are not interchangeable

Core ideas
repartition() triggers a full shuffle to redistribute data — it can increase or decrease partition count, and it's what's needed when the shuffle key itself is skewed
coalesce() merges existing partitions without a full shuffle — cheaper, but it can only reduce partition count, and it doesn't fix an uneven distribution, only a partition-count mismatch
Partition pruning lets Spark skip entire partitions of a partitioned table when a query's filter excludes them — a physical-layout decision, distinct from repartition()/coalesce()'s in-job shuffling
WHY IT MATTERS
Pinnacle's five mega-carriers account for 60%+ of shipment volume — repartitioning by carrier_id without addressing that skew just relocates the same lopsided distribution, it doesn't fix it
coalesce() would have been the wrong fix here even if someone had tried it — it can't redistribute an uneven key, only reduce the number of output partitions
Choosing the wrong one doesn't error — it just leaves the same bottleneck in place, or silently reduces parallelism further

## Skewed partitions, and what AQE's skew-join split actually does about them

SKEWED — 5 CARRIERS, 60%+ OF ROWS
AQE SKEW-JOIN SPLIT
A few oversized partitions dominate total job time
Oversized partitions split into more, evenly-sized pieces
MORE NODES DOESN'T SHRINK THE BIGGEST PARTITION
Job time is bounded by the slowest partition, not the average. Adding cluster capacity elsewhere doesn't touch that bottleneck — the fix has to address the skew itself: AQE's skew-join optimization, or manual salting when that isn't enough.

## A definition is only as trustworthy as everywhere it's actually used

Core ideas
A business-logic definition (like “on-time”) is a decision, not a fact — Pinnacle's old definition measured against end-of-calendar-day; the current one measures against the contracted hourly delivery window
Every place a definition is used has to be found and updated when it changes — there's no mechanism that does this automatically unless the logic lives in exactly one place (chapter 08)
Historical data computed under an old definition needs a stated policy — recompute it, or footnote the discontinuity — otherwise a pre/post comparison looks like a real trend when it's actually just a definition change
WHY IT MATTERS
Pinnacle's twelve notebooks show exactly what happens without that discipline — nine were updated to the new definition, three quietly kept running the old one for two months
The historical on_time_rate_by_carrier table, computed under the old definition, makes any month-over-month trend look real even when it's actually just the redefinition taking effect gradually
This is a design and governance question as much as a technical one — “where does this logic live, and who's accountable for propagating a change” has to be answered before the change ships

end of calendar day
NEW DEFINITION (current)

the contracted hourly window

Every place the old definition is used has to be found and updated, and historical data needs a stated policy (recompute, or footnote the discontinuity) — otherwise a business-logic change silently corrupts every comparison that crosses it.

## The fix chapter 07 was building toward: one module, not twelve copies

Core ideas
Files in Repos and shared Python modules let a team define logic once — a function like on_time_rate(shipments, definition_version) — and import it from every caller instead of copying it
A shared module can be unit-tested in isolation, the same way any Python function can — Pinnacle's twelve notebook-embedded copies never had that option
Version control on the shared module means every change is reviewed and has a history — not a silent edit buried inside one notebook cell among many
WHY IT MATTERS
This is the structural fix to chapter 07's propagation problem — a definition change made in on_time_rate.py reaches the SQL view, the PySpark job, and every notebook caller at once, not twelve separate times
The trade-off is real and worth naming: a shared module needs versioning and review discipline a personal notebook cell doesn't — less individual editing freedom, in exchange for the guarantee that a change actually propagates

title: T05 · Delta Lake, Performance, Compute & Cost Optimization

lessons.title: Delta Lake Internals & ACID & File Statistics & Data Skipping
lessons.body:
## Your learning goal

Diagnose Delta, Spark, compute and cost behavior from evidence — file statistics, execution plans, Spark UI metrics — not guesswork or reflexively adding capacity

## Practice case

The following organization is an illustrative training case from the supplied deck.

## Every symptom had a cause — nobody had looked closely enough to find it

Northgate is a product-analytics SaaS company — billions of usage events stream daily into events_bronze, a Delta table that has accumulated tens of millions of tiny files over years of high-frequency writes with no maintenance ever run
The nightly daily_active_users aggregation job takes 4+ hours and often spills to disk — the team's response has consistently been to add more worker nodes, which barely helps and adds cost, because nobody has opened the Spark UI's stage detail to see where the time actually goes
A Python UDF that enriches each event with a device-classification lookup accounts for a large share of the runtime — serialized row-by-row through a JVM-to-Python round trip, when the same lookup could be a broadcast join or a built-in function
Every workload — a 2-minute ad hoc query, the 4-hour nightly job, a lightweight BI dashboard refresh — runs on the same large, always-on classic cluster, because “that's the cluster we have,” regardless of whether serverless or a smaller cluster would actually fit and cost less
Finance flagged a 40% month-over-month increase in Databricks spend with no corresponding increase in data volume or business value — nobody could explain where the money was going, because nobody had broken DBU consumption out by workload

## Evidence before action, on every one of the four problems

File statistics and OPTIMIZE + liquid clustering on events_bronze, keyed on the columns actually queried — tens of millions of tiny files consolidate into right-sized ones, and data skipping starts actually working
The Spark UI's stage detail page is checked first, not cluster size — spill and skew are diagnosed from shuffle read/write size, task duration skew and spill bytes, not “add more workers” as a reflex
The device-classification UDF is replaced with a broadcast join against the small reference table — removing the Python serialization tax entirely, with no per-row process boundary left to cross
Compute is matched to workload: serverless SQL for ad hoc queries and the BI refresh, a properly sized autoscaling job cluster only for the nightly run — not one big always-on cluster for everything
DBU consumption is broken out and tagged by workload, so the next spend increase is attributable before it becomes a quarter-over-quarter surprise finance has to chase down

## The transaction log is what makes a Delta table more than a folder of Parquet files

Core ideas
A Delta table is its Parquet data files plus its _delta_log/ directory of ordered JSON commit files — the log, not the files alone, defines what the table currently contains
Each commit is atomic: it either fully succeeds and becomes the new latest version, or it doesn't happen at all — there's no partially-applied state a reader can see
Concurrent writers use optimistic concurrency control — a writer checks for conflicts at commit time and retries or fails cleanly, rather than silently corrupting or interleaving with another writer's change
WHY IT MATTERS
Every later subtopic in this module reads or writes through this same log — file statistics (03) live in it, OPTIMIZE and liquid clustering (04) rewrite entries in it, and VACUUM only removes files the log no longer references
Understanding the log is what makes “what version is this table at, and how did it get there” answerable, instead of a black box
This is the foundation candidates need before the next seven subtopics start layering performance and cost reasoning on top of it

## Data files, the log, and what each ACID guarantee actually means here

PARQUET DATA FILES
The actual columnar data —
immutable once written
_delta_log/  ·  JSON COMMIT FILES
000000.json, 000001.json, ... —
each one an atomic, ordered transaction
A TABLE = ITS DATA FILES + ITS LOG, READ TOGETHER  ·  THE LATEST COMMIT DEFINES THE CURRENT SNAPSHOT
ACID GUARANTEES — WHAT EACH ONE ACTUALLY MEANS FOR A DELTA TABLE
GUARANTEE
WHAT IT MEANS HERE
Atomicity
A write either commits as a whole new log entry, or it doesn't happen at all — no partial writes visible
Consistency
Every reader sees a table that satisfies its schema and constraints — never a half-written state
Isolation
Concurrent writers use optimistic concurrency control — a conflicting commit is retried or rejected, not interleaved
Durability
Once a commit's JSON file is written, the change survives — it's in the log, not just in memory

## Min/max stats per file, and a query that skips most of them entirely

EACH FILE CARRIES MIN/MAX STATISTICS PER COLUMN IN THE TRANSACTION LOG
file_01
order_date: 01-03 Jan
file_02
order_date: 04-07 Jan
file_03
order_date: 22-25 Feb
file_04
order_date: 26 Feb-01 Mar
file_05
order_date: 08-11 Jan
file_06
order_date: 14-17 Mar
Teal = scanned (min/max overlaps the filter)   ·   Gray = skipped entirely, never opened
QUERY:  WHERE order_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-01-15'
WHY THIS MATTERS
Three of six files are skipped entirely on their min/max range alone — no data read, no rows scanned
This only works if statistics exist and are current, and if the query filters on the columns they're collected for — an unclustered table with stale or irrelevant stats can't skip anything, however selective the query looks

## Statistics that exist but don't help are a common, easy-to-miss failure mode

Core ideas
Statistics are collected automatically at write time for a configurable number of leading columns — a query filtering on a column outside that set gets no skipping benefit at all
A table with tens of millions of tiny files (like Northgate's events_bronze before maintenance) has tens of millions of statistics entries to evaluate — the overhead of checking them can itself become significant
Data skipping and query performance are not the same claim — a query can be “fast” because it's small, with no skipping involved at all; don't credit skipping for a speedup it didn't cause
WHY IT MATTERS
Northgate's events_bronze had statistics the whole time — the tiny-file problem wasn't a missing-statistics problem, it was a too-many-files-to-check-statistics-for problem
This is why chapter 04's OPTIMIZE and liquid clustering matter beyond “fewer files look tidier” — consolidating and clustering is what makes each file's statistics actually discriminating
A candidate who checks “do statistics exist” without checking “do they actually narrow anything down for this query's filter” will misdiagnose a skipping problem as solved when it isn't

## Apply it

Use the practice case to explain one decision these topics change. Name the requirement, an alternative and the trade-off. The three questions below check your understanding. Pass at least two to unlock the next lesson; you can retry.

Source: T05-Delta-Lake-Performance-Compute-Cost-Optimization.pptx, slides 5–6 and 9–16. Adapted for self-paced reading. Live demonstrations, hidden scenario facts and independent assessment material remain outside this course.

lessons.title: Table Maintenance & Liquid Clustering & Reading Execution Plans
lessons.body:
## Three maintenance operations, three different jobs

Core ideas
OPTIMIZE compacts many small files into fewer, right-sized ones — it doesn't change what data is clustered together, just how many files hold it
Liquid clustering keeps data clustered on chosen columns incrementally, as new data lands — replacing the older Z-ORDER and fixed-partition-column approach, which can't evolve without a full table rewrite
VACUUM removes data files no longer referenced by any retained version of the log, after the retention window — reclaiming storage without breaking time travel inside that window
WHY IT MATTERS
Northgate's events_bronze needed all three, but OPTIMIZE + liquid clustering is what actually fixes both the file-open tax and the data-skipping problem from chapter 03 — VACUUM alone would only save storage, not query time
Liquid clustering specifically fixes Northgate's problem of never having chosen a partition scheme up front — it clusters on the columns actually queried today, without requiring a full rewrite if query patterns change later
None of this is a one-time fix — a table that resumes high-frequency writes with no ongoing maintenance drifts right back toward the tiny-file problem

## Northgate's events_bronze, before and after — and what each operation is for

BEFORE — YEARS OF UNMAINTAINED STREAMING WRITES
AFTER — OPTIMIZE + LIQUID CLUSTERING
Thousands of small files per partition — every query pays a per-file-open tax
file_A
right-sized, clustered
file_B
right-sized, clustered
file_C
right-sized, clustered
Clustered automatically on the columns actually queried — no manual partition scheme to maintain
MAINTENANCE OPERATION
WHAT IT DOES
REPLACES
OPTIMIZE
Compacts small files into right-sized ones
Manual file-count monitoring
Liquid clustering
Keeps data clustered on chosen keys incrementally, as new data lands
Z-ORDER and fixed partition columns, which can't evolve without a full rewrite
VACUUM
Removes data files no longer referenced by the log, after the retention window
Unbounded storage growth from old file versions

## From a query, to a plan, to what actually ran

Core ideas
EXPLAIN shows the logical-to-physical plan Catalyst built before anything runs — the shape of the work, not yet the evidence of how it went
The Spark UI's Jobs → Stages view shows what actually happened, stage by stage, once the query runs — this is where diagnosis evidence lives, not in the plan alone
Three metrics on a stage's detail page carry most of the diagnostic weight: shuffle read/write size, task duration spread, and spill bytes
WHY IT MATTERS
Northgate's team had never opened the Spark UI's stage detail for the nightly job — they were reacting to a symptom (“it's slow”) with a guess (“add workers”) instead of reading the evidence that was already there
A plan that looks fine in EXPLAIN can still perform badly at runtime if the actual data distribution doesn't match what the optimizer assumed — this is exactly what skew (chapter 06) looks like
This is the single habit this module most wants candidates to leave with: evidence before action, on every performance or cost question

## Query → plan → Spark UI, and what to actually look at once you're there

QUERY
SQL or PySpark,
as written
EXPLAIN
Logical → physical plan,
before anything runs
SPARK UI · STAGES
What actually ran,
stage by stage
WHAT TO ACTUALLY LOOK AT ON A STAGE'S DETAIL PAGE
METRIC
WHAT IT TELLS YOU
IF IT LOOKS WRONG
Shuffle read / write size
How much data actually crossed the network for a wide transformation
Unexpectedly large — check join strategy and filter placement
Task duration (min/median/max)
Whether work is spread evenly across tasks
A few tasks far longer than the rest — skew
Spill (memory / disk) bytes
Whether a task ran out of executor memory mid-operation
Non-zero and large — undersized executors or a skewed partition
THE HABIT THIS SUBTOPIC EXISTS TO BUILD
Open the stage detail page before touching cluster size — every one of these three metrics is evidence a guess can't replace

lessons.title: Skew, Shuffle & Spill Diagnosis & UDF Overhead & Pipeline Bottlenecks
lessons.body:
## Three distinct signals, easy to conflate under one vague symptom

Core ideas
Skew: a few partitions hold far more rows than the rest — visible as a handful of tasks running far longer than the median in the Spark UI's task duration view
Shuffle: data moving across the network for a wide transformation — visible as shuffle read/write size, expensive in proportion to how much data actually has to move
Spill: a task's working set exceeds its executor's available memory and has to write to disk mid-operation — visible as non-zero, often large spill bytes on that task
WHY IT MATTERS
The three are related but not interchangeable — skew is often what makes a shuffle expensive, and it's what causes spill on the specific oversized partitions' tasks, but each is diagnosed from different evidence
Northgate's nightly job showed all three at once — the team's blanket “add workers” response addressed none of them directly, since none of the three is fixed by raw additional capacity alone
Naming which of the three is present — from evidence, not a guess — is what determines the correct fix in chapters 04, 05 and 08

## Symptom, evidence, and typical fix — side by side

SKEW
A few partitions hold far
more rows than the rest
SPARK UI EVIDENCE
Task duration: a handful of tasks
run far longer than the median
TYPICAL FIX
AQE skew-join split,
or manual salting
SHUFFLE
Data moves across the network
for a wide transformation
SPARK UI EVIDENCE
Shuffle read/write size:
unexpectedly large
TYPICAL FIX
Broadcast the small side,
filter before the shuffle
SPILL
A task's working set exceeds
its executor memory
SPARK UI EVIDENCE
Spill (memory/disk) bytes:
non-zero, often large
TYPICAL FIX
Resize executors, or reduce
the per-task working set
THE THREE ARE RELATED, NOT INTERCHANGEABLE
Skew causes spill on the oversized partitions' tasks specifically, and skew is what makes a shuffle expensive in the first place — but the fix for each is diagnosed from a different piece of evidence, not guessed from the symptom “the job is slow”

## Every row a Python UDF touches crosses a process boundary, twice

Core ideas
A row-at-a-time Python UDF means each row is serialized from the JVM, sent to a Python process, executed, serialized back, and returned — a real, measurable cost per row
Catalyst can't see inside a UDF to optimize around it — it's an opaque black box in the physical plan, unlike a native Spark SQL function or a broadcast join it can reorder and prune around
A pandas UDF (vectorized) batches rows instead of crossing the boundary once per row, and is meaningfully cheaper than a row-at-a-time UDF for the same logic — but still costs more than a native function where one exists
WHY IT MATTERS
Northgate's device-classification UDF was exactly this pattern — a simple lookup that could have been a broadcast join, paying a per-row serialization tax for no reason
A pipeline bottleneck is found the same evidence-based way as chapter 05 — whichever stage takes the largest share of total stage time in the Spark UI is the bottleneck, not whichever step looks the most complex in the source code
A UDF is sometimes genuinely necessary — a Python library with no Spark-native equivalent — but that's a reason to measure its cost explicitly, not a reason to skip measuring it

## The same lookup, two very different costs

PYTHON UDF
NATIVE SPARK SQL / BROADCAST JOIN
PER-ROW SERIALIZATION ROUND TRIP
Each row: JVM → serialize → Python process
→ execute → serialize → back to JVM
Catalyst can't see inside the UDF to optimize it —
it's an opaque black box in the physical plan
STAYS INSIDE THE JVM, CATALYST-OPTIMIZED
A broadcast join against the small reference table,
or a built-in Spark SQL function, does the same lookup
No process boundary crossed per row —
Catalyst can reorder, prune and optimize around it
WHEN A UDF IS STILL THE RIGHT CALL
SITUATION
VERDICT
The logic is a simple lookup or a built-in function can express it
Avoid the UDF — use the native function or a broadcast join
The logic genuinely needs a Python library with no Spark-native equivalent
A UDF may be the only option — but measure its cost explicitly, don't assume it's free
A pandas UDF (vectorized) is available for the same logic
Prefer it over a row-at-a-time UDF — batches rows instead of one round trip each
PIPELINE BOTTLENECKS ARE FOUND THE SAME WAY
Whichever stage takes the largest share of total stage time in the Spark UI is the bottleneck — not whichever step looks the most complex in the code

## Apply it
