lessons.title: Compute Selection: Serverless vs. Classic & Workload Compatibility & Troubleshooting Methodology & FinOps Trade-offs
lessons.body:
## Serverless and classic solve different problems — pick on purpose

Core ideas
Serverless compute starts in seconds and scales to zero when idle — it fits short, bursty, unpredictable workloads where a fixed always-on cluster would sit idle most of the time
A classic cluster, sized and tuned deliberately, fits long-running, resource-heavy, predictable workloads where dedicated compute pays for itself
Compute isolation matters separately from cost — a shared, always-on cluster mixes workloads and tenants on the same compute, which can be a real governance or noisy-neighbor problem even when it's the cheaper option on paper
WHY IT MATTERS
Northgate ran everything — a 2-minute ad hoc query and the 4-hour nightly job alike — on the same large, always-on classic cluster, paying for idle capacity most of the day
Workload compatibility has to be checked before compute type, not after — serverless has a narrower, managed environment, and a workload needing a specific runtime, init script or library version may not fit it
“It's cheaper” is not sufficient justification for a compute choice a workload can't actually run on — compatibility is a hard constraint, cost is an optimization on top of it

## Workload to compute type, and the two constraints that sit alongside cost

MATCH COMPUTE TO THE WORKLOAD — NOT ONE CLUSTER FOR EVERYTHING
WORKLOAD
FITS BEST
WHY
Ad hoc / exploratory SQL queries
Serverless SQL
Starts in seconds, scales to zero when idle — no cost for an always-on cluster nobody's querying
Lightweight BI dashboard refresh
Serverless SQL
Short, bursty, unpredictable timing — a fixed classic cluster is idle most of the time
Nightly aggregation job (predictable, heavy)
Classic job cluster, autoscaling, right-sized
Long-running and resource-heavy enough that dedicated, tuned compute pays for itself
Workload needing a specific runtime, init script or library version
Classic, with explicit compatibility check
Serverless has a narrower, managed environment — verify compatibility before assuming it fits
COMPUTE ISOLATION
A shared, always-on cluster mixes workloads and tenants on the same compute
A workload with strict isolation or governance needs (regulated data, noisy-neighbor risk) may require its own dedicated cluster even at a higher cost
WORKLOAD COMPATIBILITY, CHECKED FIRST
Confirm the workload's runtime, library and connector requirements actually run on the compute type being considered
“It's cheaper” is not sufficient justification for a compute choice a workload can't actually run on

## The decision framework, not a default

Core ideas
Is the cause of a performance problem actually known, from evidence, before proposing a fix? That question — not “what's the fastest thing to try” — decides diagnose-first vs. scale-first
Is a workload's resource profile known and stable, or still unknown or highly variable? That decides deliberate right-sizing vs. a wider default autoscale range
Every fix in this module — maintenance, join strategy, compute selection — traces back to a specific piece of evidence, not a general best practice applied blindly
WHY IT MATTERS
Every subtopic in this module is a diagnostic tool — this chapter is where candidates prove they can apply the right one under pressure, unprompted, to a scenario not yet discussed
“We added more workers” is not a defensible answer on its own — sometimes it's correct, but only once the cause is confirmed as genuinely capacity-bound, not skew, spill, or an unoptimized plan
This is the framework the guided and independent practice exercises, and the exit rubric, are scored against

## Two settings, always named and justified

THE SETTINGS
Diagnose-first (read the evidence) vs. scale-first (add capacity) — the evidence-known-or-not question from this chapter
Deliberate right-sizing vs. a wide default autoscale range — the profile-stable-or-not question
WHAT A STRONG DEFENSE SOUNDS LIKE
Names the specific setting, states both sides of the trade-off, and points at the evidence that tips it
“We diagnosed skew from the task duration spread before adding capacity, because Northgate's job was skewed, not undersized” — not “we made it faster”
FinOps choices (compute selection, autoscale range, maintenance cadence) belong here too — they're cost/complexity decisions, not just mechanical ones

## Two concrete decisions candidates must be able to defend

DIAGNOSE FIRST, VS. SCALE FIRST
RIGHT-SIZE, VS. DEFAULT AUTOSCALE RANGE
Diagnose first (evidence)
Correct when the cause isn't yet known — read file stats and the Spark UI's stage detail before changing anything
Scale first (add capacity)
Correct only once the cause IS known and is genuinely capacity-bound, not skew, spill or an unoptimized plan
Right-size deliberately
Correct when a workload's resource profile is known and stable — sized to the evidence, not a guess
Wide default autoscale range
Correct when a workload's profile is still unknown or highly variable — costs more per hour but avoids under-provisioning blind
THE DEFENSIBLE ANSWER NAMES THE EVIDENCE, NOT A HABIT
“We added more workers” and “we always use the widest autoscale range” are both myths for a diagnosis-first team — name what the Spark UI or file statistics actually showed, and what it specifically pointed to before choosing

## Apply it

Use the practice case to explain one decision these topics change. Name the requirement, an alternative and the trade-off. The three questions below check your understanding. Pass at least two to unlock the next lesson; you can retry.

title: T06 · Unity Catalog, Security & Data Governance

lessons.title: Catalog & Schema Architecture & Permissions & Access Control
lessons.body:
## Your learning goal

Design catalog structure, least-privilege access, lineage, auditing, PII controls, federation and external sharing as one coherent enterprise governance pattern — not eight separate settings

## Practice case

The following organization is an illustrative training case from the supplied deck.

## One shared catalog, no boundaries, and a governed-access audit six weeks away

Wrenfield is a pharmaceutical company with three business units — R&D, Clinical, and Commercial — all reading and writing through a single shared Unity Catalog catalog, with no schema or catalog boundary separating them
Most teams were granted broad, workspace-admin-level access early on “to get moving,” and nobody has since scoped it down — a Commercial analyst can query R&D's unreleased compound data without anyone noticing
There is no lineage tracking and no centralized audit log — nobody can say with confidence which reports depend on which source tables, or who accessed a given patient record and when
Patient and trial data containing PII (patient IDs, SSNs) sits untagged and unmasked in the same tables analysts query daily — there is no distinction between what a Clinical analyst and a Compliance officer should each be able to see
Wrenfield shares trial data with an external contract research organization (CRO) via manually emailed spreadsheet exports — ungoverned, unaudited, and increasingly the thing Legal is most worried about ahead of a regulatory review

## Governance by design, on every one of the five gaps

A catalog per business unit — separate R&D, Clinical and Commercial catalogs, each with its own schemas — replacing the single flat metastore with structure that maps to how Wrenfield actually organizes work
Grants scoped to least privilege at every level (catalog, schema, table), replacing broad workspace-admin access with exactly the USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT privileges each team actually needs
Lineage turned on and used as a live impact-analysis tool, so a schema change or a PII question can be answered by querying the graph instead of asking every team by hand
PII columns tagged once as governed data, with column masks and row filters applied at query time — Analysts and Compliance officers query the same table and see different values, with no separate masked copy to maintain
The CRO's manual spreadsheet exports replaced with a governed Delta Share — access is grant-based, auditable, and revocable, with no credential file or unsecured attachment involved

## The three-level namespace is a design surface, not just a naming convention

Core ideas
Every Unity Catalog object has a three-level address — catalog.schema.table — and each level is a real boundary that grants, workspace bindings and most other controls scope against
A catalog typically maps to a business unit or an environment (dev/staging/prod); a schema typically maps to a team or a subject area within it — the layout should mirror how the organization actually splits work, not be an afterthought
Catalogs and schemas can be created and restructured after the fact, but a flat, single-catalog layout (like Wrenfield's) makes every later control — grants, workspace isolation, lineage scoping — harder to reason about than it needs to be
WHY IT MATTERS
Wrenfield's single shared catalog is why a Commercial analyst could query R&D's unreleased data without anyone deciding that should be possible — the boundary that would have prevented it was never drawn
Every later subtopic in this module scopes against this layout — workspace bindings (04) bind a workspace to a catalog, not to individual tables; grants (03) are usually issued at the catalog or schema level, not table by table
Getting the catalog/schema layout right first is what makes every later governance decision simpler, not just more correct

## The three-level namespace, and Wrenfield's catalog-per-business-unit layout

THE THREE-LEVEL NAMESPACE — EVERY TABLE HAS A FULL ADDRESS
CATALOG
wrenfield_clinical
a business unit or environment
SCHEMA
trial_data
a team or subject area within it
TABLE
patient_outcomes
the actual dataset
WRENFIELD'S CATALOG-PER-BUSINESS-UNIT LAYOUT
R&D CATALOG
schema: genomics
schema: compound_library
CLINICAL CATALOG
schema: trial_data
schema: adverse_events
COMMERCIAL CATALOG
schema: sales
schema: market_access
WHY THIS MATTERS
A catalog boundary is what a workspace binding (chapter 04) and most grants (chapter 03) actually scope — get this layout right first, or every later control inherits the same flat structure it was meant to fix

## USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are gates — SELECT is what actually reads data

Core ideas
A grant is issued to a principal (a user, a service principal, or a group) on a securable object (a catalog, schema, table, view, volume or function) for a specific privilege
USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are entry gates — they let a principal reference objects at that level at all, but grant no read access on their own; SELECT is the privilege that actually reads rows, and is itself subject to any row filter or column mask defined on the table
Least privilege means granting exactly the privileges a role needs, at the narrowest scope that covers it — not granting broad access “to get moving” and planning to scope it down later, which at Wrenfield never actually happened
WHY IT MATTERS
Wrenfield's workspace-admin-level grants were exactly this shortcut — broad access issued early, under time pressure, never revisited once the urgency passed
A principal needs the right privilege at every level in the path — USE CATALOG on the catalog, USE SCHEMA on the schema, and SELECT on the table — which is what makes “grant everyone admin on the metastore” a single point of failure rather than a convenience
This is the mechanism every later fix in this module has to work through — a schema restructure (02) or a workspace binding (04) doesn't help if the underlying grants still hand out broad access regardless

## Principal, privilege, securable object — and the privileges that carry the most weight

PRINCIPAL
A user, service principal,
or group
GRANT <privilege>
e.g. SELECT, USE SCHEMA,
CREATE TABLE
SECURABLE OBJECT
Catalog, schema, table,
view, volume, or function
COMMON PRIVILEGES AND WHAT EACH ONE ACTUALLY UNLOCKS
PRIVILEGE
WHAT IT UNLOCKS
USE CATALOG
Lets a principal reference objects inside the catalog at all — the entry gate, grants nothing on its own
USE SCHEMA
Lets a principal reference objects inside a specific schema — same entry-gate role, one level down
SELECT
Read rows from a table or view — subject to any row filter or column mask defined on it
MODIFY / CREATE TABLE
Write to existing data, or create new objects inside a schema the principal already has USE SCHEMA on
GRANTS ARE ADDITIVE AND SCOPE-SPECIFIC
USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA are gates, not read access by themselves — a principal needs the right privilege at every level in the path, which is exactly what makes “grant everyone admin on the metastore” the wrong shortcut, not a convenience

## Apply it

Use the practice case to explain one decision these topics change. Name the requirement, an alternative and the trade-off. The three questions below check your understanding. Pass at least two to unlock the next lesson; you can retry.

Source: T06-Unity-Catalog-Security-Data-Governance.pptx, slides 5–6 and 9–16. Adapted for self-paced reading. Live demonstrations, hidden scenario facts and independent assessment material remain outside this course.

lessons.title: Workspace Isolation & Data Lineage
lessons.body:
## One account metastore, many workspaces, each scoped to its own catalogs

Core ideas
A Unity Catalog metastore is shared across every workspace in the account — but a workspace-catalog binding restricts which catalogs a given workspace can actually see and use
Workspace isolation is a hard boundary enforced independently of grants — a principal with a valid SELECT grant on a catalog still can't reach it from a workspace that isn't bound to that catalog
Isolation typically maps to the same business-unit or environment split as the catalog layout (02) — a workspace per business unit, each bound only to its own catalog, is a common enterprise pattern
WHY IT MATTERS
Wrenfield ran all three business units out of one shared workspace with no binding restrictions — even after fixing grants and catalog structure, a misconfigured or overly broad grant could still be exercised from anywhere
Workspace isolation is what turns “this data belongs to R&D” from a policy statement into something enforced by the platform even if a grant is ever issued too broadly by mistake
This is a defense-in-depth layer, not a replacement for correct grants (03) — both need to be right together

## One metastore, three workspaces, each bound only to its own catalog

ONE ACCOUNT METASTORE — SHARED ACROSS ALL WORKSPACES
R&D WORKSPACE
bound only to the
R&D catalog
CLINICAL WORKSPACE

COMMERCIAL WORKSPACE
bound only to the
Commercial catalog
EACH WORKSPACE CAN ONLY SEE THE CATALOGS IT'S BOUND TO
R&D catalog
Clinical catalog
Commercial catalog
WHY THIS MATTERS
A workspace-catalog binding is a hard boundary, not a UI convenience — even a principal with a valid grant on the Clinical catalog can't reach it from the R&D workspace unless that binding explicitly allows it

## Captured automatically, every time data moves through a query or a job

Core ideas
Unity Catalog captures lineage automatically at the table and column level for any query, notebook or job that reads from one governed table and writes to another — no manual tagging or diagramming required
Lineage is a graph, not a list — it answers “which downstream tables and dashboards does this source table (or this specific column) reach,” which is exactly the impact-analysis question a schema change or a PII question both need answered
Lineage is descriptive, not preventative — it shows what depends on what; it doesn't by itself restrict access (that's grants and masks) or log who read what (that's auditing)
WHY IT MATTERS
Wrenfield had no lineage tracking, so “which reports depend on this patient table” was a question someone had to answer by asking every team by hand — slow, and only as reliable as who remembered to reply
Column-level lineage is what makes a PII question like “which dashboards ultimately show this SSN column” answerable directly, rather than requiring a code-repo-by-code-repo audit
This is the evidence a regulator actually wants during a data-flow review — the graph itself, generated automatically, not a diagram reconstructed from memory under audit pressure

## Source, transformation, downstream table, dashboard — traced automatically, column by column

LINEAGE IS CAPTURED AUTOMATICALLY, COLUMN BY COLUMN, EVERY TIME DATA MOVES
raw_patient_intake
Source table,
patient_id tagged PII

patient_id still present
Enrollment Dashboard
A BI report built
on top of it

WHAT LINEAGE ACTUALLY MAKES POSSIBLE
USE CASE
WITHOUT LINEAGE
WITH LINEAGE

Query the graph — every downstream consumer is listed
Tracing a PII column's blast radius
Guess, or audit code repo by repo
Column-level lineage shows every table and dashboard it reaches
Regulatory data-flow evidence
Reconstruct by memory under audit pressure
The graph itself is the evidence, generated automatically

lessons.title: Auditing & Monitoring & PII & Privacy Controls
lessons.body:
## system.access.audit is a table — query it like one

Core ideas
Unity Catalog logs governed actions — reads, grants, schema changes, drops — centrally and automatically, with no per-table opt-in required
The audit log is exposed as queryable system tables, not a file a platform team has to export on request — “who accessed what, and when” is a SQL query away
Auditing is a record of what happened; it doesn't by itself prevent anything — it's the evidence layer that sits alongside grants (prevention), lineage (structure) and PII controls (masking)
WHY IT MATTERS
Wrenfield had no centralized audit log — “who accessed this patient record last month” had no answer at all, which is exactly the kind of gap a regulatory review is designed to find
Because the log is a system table, it can be joined against lineage or grant history for a fuller picture — e.g. “which of the principals who can currently SELECT this table have actually queried it in the last 90 days”
This is what makes a compliance review a query instead of a week of reconstructing access history from memory and scattered notes

## User action → Unity Catalog → system tables, queryable like any other table

USER ACTION
A query, a grant,
a table read or drop
UNITY CATALOG
Every governed action
is logged centrally
SYSTEM TABLES
system.access.audit —
queryable like any table
A QUERY AGAINST THE AUDIT LOG ANSWERS: WHO ACCESSED WHAT, AND WHEN
PRINCIPAL
ACTION
OBJECT
WHEN

WHY THIS MATTERS
Every governed action is logged automatically — nobody has to remember to enable it per table, and the log itself is queryable SQL, not a file to request from a platform team days before an audit

## Tag once, mask at query time — the same table, different results per role

Core ideas
A governed tag (data classification) marks a column as PII once, centrally — that classification is what a column mask or row filter policy checks against, rather than each policy re-deciding what counts as sensitive
A column mask applies a function to a tagged column's value at query time, based on who's asking — an Analyst and a Compliance officer query the identical table and see different results, computed live, not from two different tables
A row filter restricts which rows a principal can see at all, evaluated per query — distinct from a column mask, which restricts what a visible row's column shows
WHY IT MATTERS
Wrenfield's PII sat untagged and unmasked in the same tables analysts query daily — there was no way to give an Analyst useful access without also handing them a compliance officer's view of the data
Because masking happens at query time against the single source table, there's no separately-maintained “masked copy” that can drift out of sync with the real data or get forgotten during a schema change
This is the mechanism that makes “broad SELECT access, safely” possible — the grant can be broad because the mask, not the grant, is what limits what's actually visible

## The same table, tagged and masked — different roles see different values

THE SAME TABLE, TAGGED AND MASKED — DIFFERENT ROLES SEE DIFFERENT VALUES
ANALYST VIEW (masked)
patient_id: ****-4471
ssn: MASKED

COMPLIANCE VIEW (unmasked)
patient_id: PT-118842-4471
ssn: full value visible
diagnosis_code: J45.909
THE THREE CONTROLS THAT MAKE THIS WORK
CONTROL
WHAT IT DOES
Governed tag / data classification
Marks a column as PII (e.g. SSN, patient_id) once, centrally — the classification a mask or filter policy checks against
Column mask
Applies a function to a tagged column's value at query time, based on who's asking — same table, different result per role
Row filter
Restricts which rows a principal can see at all, evaluated per query — not a separate filtered copy of the table
ONE TABLE, NOT A MASKED COPY
The masking and filtering happen at query time against the single source table — there's no separately-maintained “safe” copy to keep in sync or forget to update

## Apply it

lessons.title: Data Federation & Delta Sharing & Enterprise Governance Patterns
lessons.body:
## Lakehouse Federation extends Unity Catalog's governance to data it doesn't own

Core ideas
A foreign catalog registers an external system (Postgres, Snowflake, MySQL and others) inside Unity Catalog, so its tables can be queried through the same three-level namespace and the same grant model as any native table
Federation queries the external system live, at query time — there's no copy landed in Databricks, so the data is never stale between syncs and there's no second place the same PII has to be governed all over again
Federation is a query-time bridge, not a replacement for ingestion — it re-queries the source system on every access, which doesn't scale to high-volume, repeated joins the way a landed, ingested copy would
WHY IT MATTERS
Wrenfield's CRO-facing data currently flows the opposite direction (Wrenfield sharing out, not querying in), but the same live-in-place principle is exactly what avoids the “now we have two places to govern the same data” problem — see chapter 09's federation-vs-Delta-Sharing distinction
A workload needing occasional lookups against a small external table is a strong federation fit; a workload doing high-volume repeated joins against the same external data is not — that's a judgment call, not a default
Federated tables inherit Unity Catalog's grants, masks and audit logging — a foreign catalog isn't a governance exception, it's the same governance model extended outward

## Copy-then-query vs. query-in-place, and when each pattern actually fits

OLD PATTERN — COPY, THEN QUERY
FEDERATION — QUERY IN PLACE
ETL JOB COPIES THE CRO'S POSTGRES DATA IN
A nightly job extracts and lands a copy in Databricks —
stale between runs, and now a second place
the same PII has to be governed all over again
FOREIGN CATALOG POINTS AT THE LIVE SYSTEM
A query reads the CRO's Postgres table directly,
through Unity Catalog's own grants —
no copy, no separate governance to maintain
WHEN TO REACH FOR FEDERATION VS. INGESTION
SITUATION
BETTER FIT
Occasional lookups against a small, low-latency-tolerant external table
Federation — no pipeline to build or maintain for infrequent access
High-volume, repeated joins against the same external data
Ingestion — federation re-queries the source system every time, which doesn't scale to heavy repeated use
The external system's data needs Databricks-side transformation, quality checks, or history
Ingestion — federation only reads; it doesn't materialize or version the data

## Sharing out, governed, replacing the manual export entirely

Core ideas
Delta Sharing lets Wrenfield grant a recipient read access to a live share of its own governed data — the recipient sees current data with no copy re-sent on every update, and access can be revoked centrally at any time
Open sharing (a credential file and any Delta Sharing client) fits a recipient with no Databricks account at all; Databricks-to-Databricks sharing fits a recipient who has their own Unity Catalog metastore — grant-based, no credential file to secure or rotate
Delta Sharing and federation move data in opposite directions — Delta Sharing is Wrenfield pushing its own governed data out; federation (chapter 08) is Wrenfield pulling someone else's data in — the two are not interchangeable
WHY IT MATTERS
Wrenfield's manual spreadsheet exports to the CRO are exactly what Delta Sharing replaces — access becomes grant-based, auditable and revocable instead of an unsecured attachment nobody can take back once it's sent
Choosing open sharing vs. Databricks-to-Databricks is a real design decision, not a default — it depends entirely on whether the recipient (the CRO, in Wrenfield's case) has their own Databricks presence
This is the external-facing capstone of everything else in this module — catalog structure, grants, PII tagging and masks all have to be correct before it makes sense to extend access outside the organization at all

## Two settings, always named and justified

THE SETTINGS
Delta Sharing (push out) vs. federation (pull in) — which direction does the data actually need to move, and who owns it
Open sharing vs. Databricks-to-Databricks — does the recipient have their own Unity Catalog metastore or not
WHAT A STRONG DEFENSE SOUNDS LIKE
Names the specific setting, states both sides of the trade-off, and points at the fact that tips it
“We used Databricks-to-Databricks sharing because the CRO already runs its own Unity Catalog metastore — grant-based access with no credential file to secure” — not “we shared it with Delta Sharing”
Enterprise governance patterns belong here too — catalog structure, least privilege, workspace isolation, lineage, auditing and PII controls are one composed pattern, not eight independent checkboxes to tick separately

## Two concrete decisions candidates must be able to defend

DELTA SHARING VS. FEDERATION
OPEN SHARING VS. DATABRICKS-TO-DATABRICKS
Delta Sharing (push out)
Wrenfield owns the data and grants a recipient read access to a live share — correct for publishing Wrenfield's own governed data to the CRO
Federation (pull in)
Wrenfield queries someone else's system in place — correct for reading data Wrenfield doesn't own and won't host
Open sharing
Correct when the recipient (the CRO) has no Databricks account at all — they read via a credential file and any Delta Sharing client
Databricks-to-Databricks
Correct when the recipient has their own Unity Catalog metastore — sharing is grant-based, no credential file to secure or rotate
ENTERPRISE GOVERNANCE PATTERNS — THE SYNTHESIS
Catalog structure, least-privilege grants, workspace isolation, lineage, auditing and PII controls aren't independent checkboxes — they compose into one coherent pattern, and Delta Sharing is what extends that same pattern to a recipient outside the organization, rather than falling back to an ungoverned file export

## Apply it

title: T07 · Software Engineering, DevOps & Deployment Automation

lessons.title: Project Structure, Git & VS Code & Testing
lessons.body:
## Your learning goal

Convert Databricks solutions into tested, automated and repeatably deployed engineering products — project structure, testing, CI/CD, deployment-as-code, environment promotion and secure integrations as one coherent practice

## Practice case

The following organization is an illustrative training case from the supplied deck.

## A fraud-detection pipeline held together by naming conventions and hope

Solmark is a fast-growing fintech whose fraud-detection pipeline lives entirely in a dozen interdependent notebooks in one shared workspace folder, with no Git history beyond manually-named “backup” copies
There is no automated testing — every change is validated by a data scientist manually re-running cells and eyeballing the output before pushing to production
Deploying a change means clicking through the workspace UI by hand against whichever environment happens to be open, with no dev/staging/production separation and no reliable way to undo a bad release
The fraud-scoring API, the finance team's BI dashboards, and the on-call Slack alerting are all wired up with hardcoded personal access tokens belonging to engineers who have since left
A recent outage took four hours to diagnose and roll back, because nobody could say for certain which notebook version was actually running in production

## Engineering discipline, on every one of the five gaps

Fraud-detection logic extracted into a proper Git repo with a src/ package and a pytest test suite, replacing “backup” copies with real version history
A CI/CD pipeline in GitHub Actions runs lint and the full test suite on every pull request, and only a tagged, reviewed release reaches production
Databricks Asset Bundles define jobs and pipelines once, deployed identically (different targets) to dev, staging and production — with rollback meaning “redeploy the last known-good tag,” not a scramble
Every API, BI, and alerting integration authenticated through a scoped service principal instead of a departed engineer's personal token
A four-hour blind outage becomes a known-version rollback measured in minutes, because the deployed version is always traceable to a specific tagged commit

## The structure a maintained project needs, and where each tool fits

Core ideas
A Databricks project maintained by more than one person needs the same structure any software project needs — a src/ package for importable logic, a tests/ folder, resource definitions, and a databricks.yml bundle config — not one notebook with everything inline
Git is the source of truth for the code's history — branches, pull requests, and diffs — not the workspace's own notebook revision history, which tracks cell contents but not intent or review
VS Code with the Databricks extension (using Databricks Connect) lets a developer edit locally and run code against a real cluster without the code ever having to “live” in the browser notebook UI; Databricks Repos then syncs that same Git repo into the workspace so notebooks and files stay tied to source control
WHY IT MATTERS
Solmark's twelve interdependent notebooks with “backup” naming are exactly what this structure replaces — there was no answer to “what changed, and why” beyond asking whoever wrote it
This is the foundation every later subtopic in this module builds on — testing (03) needs importable functions to test, CI/CD (04) needs a repo to run against, and Asset Bundles (05) need a databricks.yml to deploy
Getting the project structure right first is what makes every later engineering practice possible, not just tidier

## Before: one notebook, everything inline. After: a repo with a real structure.

BEFORE: ONE NOTEBOOK, EVERYTHING INLINE
Transformation logic, config, and one-off
test cells all mixed into a single .ipynb,
edited directly in the browser, no history
beyond "Notebook (2) (copy)"
AFTER: A REPO WITH A REAL STRUCTURE
src/ — importable transformation modules
tests/ — pytest unit tests
resources/ — job & pipeline definitions
databricks.yml — the bundle config
TOOL
ROLE IN THIS WORKFLOW
Git
Version history, branches, pull requests — the source of truth for the code, not the workspace
VS Code + Databricks extension
Local editing with Databricks Connect, so code runs against a real cluster without living in the browser
Databricks Repos
Syncs the same Git repo into the workspace, so notebooks and files stay tied to source control

## Fast unit tests and cluster-real integration tests, together

Core ideas
A unit test (pytest, no cluster) validates a function's logic in isolation, in seconds, and should run on every save — it's the fast, cheap gate that catches broken logic before anything touches Databricks at all
An integration test (via Databricks Connect) runs the same code against a real cluster, catching cluster-dependent behavior — actual Spark execution, real table reads/writes — that a pure unit test can't see
Both gates have to pass before a change can merge; neither substitutes for the other — a unit-test-only suite misses cluster-dependent bugs, and an integration-test-only suite is too slow to run on every small change
WHY IT MATTERS
Solmark's only “test” was a data scientist manually re-running cells and eyeballing the output — subjective, unrepeatable, and skipped entirely under time pressure
This is what a CI/CD pipeline (chapter 04) actually runs — without a real test suite, “the pipeline ran green” means nothing
Confusing a fast unit-test suite with full coverage is a common trap — a candidate should be able to say specifically what a unit test does and doesn't catch

## Code change → local unit tests → CI integration tests → merge

CODE CHANGE
A transformation function
is edited locally
LOCAL UNIT TESTS
pytest runs against the
function's pure logic
CI INTEGRATION TESTS
Databricks Connect runs it
against a real cluster
MERGE
Only a change that passes
both gates reaches main
TEST TYPE
WHAT IT CATCHES
WHAT IT MISSES
Unit test (pytest, no cluster)
Broken logic in a single function, in seconds, on every save
Anything that only breaks against real Databricks Connect or cluster behavior
Integration test (Databricks Connect)
Cluster-dependent behavior — Spark execution, real table reads/writes
Slower to run — not the right tool for every small logic change

## Apply it

lessons.title: CI/CD & GitHub Actions & Databricks Asset Bundles
lessons.body:
## Automating what a human used to do by hand — and only by hand, inconsistently

Core ideas
A CI/CD pipeline automates what a human used to do by hand: on every push or pull request, GitHub Actions triggers automatically, runs lint and the full test suite, and only a tagged, reviewed release reaches production — no manual kickoff, no skipped step under time pressure
Different triggers should do different things: a pull request runs validation only (nothing deployed); a merge to main deploys to staging; a tagged release deploys to production — deliberately, not automatically on every merge
The Databricks CLI (via databricks bundle deploy) is what a GitHub Actions workflow actually calls to perform a deployment — CI/CD is the automation wrapper around the same bundle deploy a developer could run locally
WHY IT MATTERS
Solmark's “deploy” was a person clicking through the workspace UI by hand against whichever environment happened to be open — CI/CD is the direct fix, removing the human as the single point of failure and inconsistency
This is what actually enforces chapter 03's testing discipline — a test suite that isn't run automatically on every change is a test suite that gets skipped exactly when it matters most, under deadline pressure
Production deploying only on a tagged release (not every merge) is a deliberate design choice, not caution for its own sake — it's the last human decision point before a change reaches customers

## Push/PR → GitHub Actions → lint + test → build & deploy bundle

PUSH / PULL REQUEST
A branch is pushed or
a PR is opened
GITHUB ACTIONS WORKFLOW
Triggered automatically —
no manual kickoff
LINT + TEST
Unit tests and integration
tests both must pass
BUILD & DEPLOY BUNDLE
databricks bundle deploy
to the target environment
WORKFLOW TRIGGER
WHAT RUNS
TARGET
Pull request opened
Lint + unit tests + integration tests
None — validation only, nothing deployed
Merge to main
Full test suite, then bundle deploy
Staging — never production directly
Tagged release
Full test suite, then bundle deploy
Production — a deliberate, reviewed step

## databricks.yml as the single source of truth for what gets deployed

Core ideas
A Databricks Asset Bundle (databricks.yml) defines a project's jobs, pipelines, and other resources as code, once — not clicked together separately in each environment's UI
A bundle's targets section is what makes the same definition deploy differently per environment — dev, staging, production each point at a different workspace, schema and permission set, without duplicating the resource definitions themselves
databricks bundle deploy -t <target> is the single command that performs a deployment — the same command a developer runs locally and a CI/CD pipeline runs automatically, which is exactly what makes deployment repeatable instead of a manual, per-environment ritual
WHY IT MATTERS
Solmark's UI-click deployment was different every time, by definition — Asset Bundles are the direct fix, because the same YAML deploys the same way whether it's a developer's laptop or a GitHub Actions runner
This is the mechanism environment promotion (chapter 06) actually operates through — “promoting” a change means deploying the same bundle to a different target, not manually recreating it
Bundles version alongside the code in Git, so a rollback (chapter 06) is literally redeploying a previous Git tag's bundle — not a separate, undocumented recovery procedure

## databricks.yml, and databricks bundle deploy -t <target>

databricks.yml
bundle:
name: solmark-fraud-pipeline
targets:
dev: ...      staging: ...      prod: ...
resources:
jobs: ...     pipelines: ...
databricks bundle deploy -t <target>
One definition, deployed differently
per target — the same jobs and
pipelines, pointed at a different
workspace, schema and permission set
depending on which target is named
TARGET
WORKSPACE
MODE
dev
Developer's own workspace
development — fast iteration, no approval gate
staging
Shared pre-production workspace
validation — mirrors production config
prod
Production workspace
production — locked permissions, deploy on tag only

questions.prompt: What's the difference between what happens on a pull request vs. a merge to main in a well-designed pipeline?

options.label: Both trigger a full production rollback
There's no difference — both deploy to production

lessons.title: Environment Promotion & REST APIs, SDKs & Authentication
lessons.body:
## Dev → staging → production, each with a checked gate, and a tested path back

Core ideas
Promotion means deploying the same bundle to progressively more production-like targets — dev (fast iteration) → staging (mirrors production configuration) → production (locked permissions, deploy on tag only) — not rewriting anything between stages
A promotion gate is a checked condition, not a formality: dev → staging requires the full test suite to pass in CI and a reviewer to approve the pull request; staging → production requires staging validation to pass and the release to be deliberately tagged
Rollback means redeploying the previous tagged bundle version — a known-good, already-tested state — not a hand-edit made directly in production under incident pressure
WHY IT MATTERS
Solmark's outage took four hours to diagnose specifically because there was no reliable way to know which version was live, let alone redeploy a known-good one — environment promotion with tagged rollback is the direct fix
This is where chapters 04 and 05 actually connect — CI/CD (04) is what triggers a promotion, and Asset Bundles (05) are what gets promoted; environment promotion is the discipline that governs when and how that happens
A rollback that's just “redeploy the last tag” is fast and safe precisely because it's already been tested — a forward-fix under incident pressure risks shipping a second untested change on top of the first problem

## Dev → staging → production, and the rollback path back

DEV
Fast iteration,
one bundle target per developer
STAGING
Same bundle, staging target —
the last check before production
PRODUCTION
Deploy on tagged release only —
locked permissions, no ad hoc edits
← rollback: redeploy the previous tagged bundle version, not a hand edit in production
PROMOTION GATE
WHAT IT CHECKS
Dev → Staging
Full test suite passes in CI, reviewer approves the pull request
Staging → Production
Staging validation passes, release is tagged deliberately — not automatic on every merge

## Every API call authenticates as some identity — and the identity matters

Core ideas
The Databricks REST API (and the databricks-sdk client libraries built on top of it) let a script, app, or CI job act on a Databricks workspace programmatically — starting a job, reading a table's metadata, managing a cluster — the same actions a person could do in the UI, callable from code
Every API call authenticates as some identity, and the identity matters: a personal access token (PAT) is tied to an individual and best suited to interactive, individual use; OAuth is the modern default for both interactive apps and automation; a service principal is a non-human identity purpose-built for CI/CD, scheduled jobs, and unattended automation
A service principal is the correct identity for automation specifically because it isn't tied to a person — it keeps working (or can be deliberately revoked) independent of who's employed, and it can be scoped to exactly the permissions the automation needs, no more
WHY IT MATTERS
Solmark's fraud-API and alerting integrations were authenticated with personal access tokens belonging to engineers who have since left — exactly the failure mode a service principal exists to prevent
This is the authentication layer every integration in chapter 08 (BI connectivity, operational integrations) actually depends on — a webhook or a BI tool's connection is only as safe as the credential behind it
Treating “it still works” as proof an integration is set up correctly is a trap — a token tied to a departed engineer often keeps working right up until it's revoked or expires, silently

## Client → SDK or REST call → authentication → workspace API

CLIENT
A script, app, or
CI job
SDK OR REST CALL
databricks-sdk, or a
direct HTTPS request
AUTHENTICATION
OAuth token or a
service-principal identity
WORKSPACE API
The action executes as
that authenticated identity
AUTH METHOD
FITS
RISK IF MISUSED
Personal access token (PAT)
Interactive, individual use — not automation
Tied to a person; keeps working after they leave unless revoked
OAuth (user or machine)
Interactive apps and modern automation
Short-lived by design — the safer default for new integrations
Service principal
CI/CD, scheduled jobs, unattended automation
Not tied to a person — the correct identity for a pipeline, not a shared human token

lessons.title: BI Connectivity & Operational Integrations & Engineering Patterns & Deployment Trade-offs
lessons.body:
## Two directions: BI tools query in, operational systems react out

Core ideas
BI connectivity runs through a Databricks SQL warehouse via a JDBC/ODBC driver — the warehouse, not a notebook, is the governed, concurrent query endpoint a BI tool should connect to, since it's built for exactly that access pattern
Operational integrations run the other direction — a job's success or failure triggers an outbound webhook to Slack, PagerDuty, or a ticketing system, so the operational system reacts to Databricks rather than Databricks waiting on it
Both integration types inherit whatever authentication method (chapter 07) is behind them — a BI connection or a webhook is only as trustworthy as the credential it authenticates with, which is why this subtopic builds directly on the previous one
WHY IT MATTERS
Solmark's finance BI dashboards and on-call Slack alerting were both wired up alongside the same hardcoded personal tokens as the fraud API — the fix is the same authentication discipline applied consistently, not a special case per integration
A BI tool querying a notebook directly (rather than a SQL warehouse) is a common anti-pattern this subtopic exists to correct — notebooks aren't built for concurrent, governed query access the way a warehouse is
This is the last mile of the architecture — everything upstream (structure, tests, CI/CD, bundles, promotion, authentication) exists so that these outward-facing integrations are actually trustworthy

## BI connectivity in, operational integrations out

BI CONNECTIVITY
Databricks SQL warehouse → JDBC/ODBC driver
→ a BI tool's own connection pool
The warehouse, not a notebook, is the
governed, concurrent query endpoint
OPERATIONAL INTEGRATIONS
A job's success/failure triggers a webhook
→ Slack, PagerDuty, or a ticketing system
The operational system reacts to Databricks;
Databricks doesn't wait on it
INTEGRATION
PROTOCOL
EXAMPLE

A dashboard tool refreshing on a schedule
Operational alerting
Outbound webhook on job event
A failed pipeline posts to an on-call Slack channel
Ticketing / workflow system

A completed reconciliation opens a review ticket automatically

## A one-time setup cost against a cost that recurs every time a shortcut is repeated

Core ideas
Asset Bundles cost real setup time upfront — a manual click-through deploy costs correctness every single time it's repeated by hand; the trade-off is a one-time cost against a recurring one
A notebook is faster to start something in; a proper package (src/ + tests/) is what actually makes testing and code review possible — the trade-off shows up the moment more than one person needs to trust the code
Redeploying the last known-good tagged bundle is the safe rollback; a forward-fix under incident pressure risks shipping a second untested change on top of the first problem — the trade-off is speed of one fix vs. the risk of two
WHY IT MATTERS
Solmark's entire failure mode was choosing the fast, informal option every time — notebooks over packages, manual deploys over bundles, personal tokens over service principals — and each individually-reasonable shortcut compounded into a four-hour blind outage
Every one of these trade-offs has a “fast now” side and a “safe and repeatable” side — the module's whole point is recognizing which one a given moment actually calls for, not defaulting to one side reflexively
This is the direct rehearsal for the defend stage — candidates must be able to name a trade-off, state both sides, and say which fact tipped it for Solmark specifically

## Two trade-offs, always named and justified

THE TRADE-OFFS
Asset Bundles vs. manual deploy — which one is actually the durable choice once more than one person or one environment is involved
Rollback vs. forward-fix — under incident pressure, which one actually reduces risk rather than adding a second untested change
WHAT A STRONG DEFENSE SOUNDS LIKE
Names the specific trade-off, states both sides, and points at the fact that tips it — not just the tool name
“We used a service principal because the fraud-API integration has to survive personnel changes and be scoped to exactly its own permissions” — not “we used a service principal because it's best practice”
Engineering maturity belongs here too — structure, tests, CI/CD, bundles, environment promotion, and authenticated integrations are one composed pattern, not independent checkboxes to tick separately

## Two concrete decisions candidates must be able to defend

Asset Bundles vs. manual deploy
Bundles cost setup time upfront; a manual click-through deploy costs correctness every single time it's repeated by hand
Notebook-first vs. package-first code
A notebook is faster to start; a proper package (src/ + tests/) is what makes testing and code review possible at all
Rollback vs. forward-fix
Redeploying the last known-good tagged bundle is fast and safe; a forward-fix under incident pressure risks shipping a second untested change
Service principal vs. personal token
A service principal survives personnel changes and scopes to exactly what the automation needs; a personal token quietly becomes a single point of failure
ENGINEERING MATURITY IS A COMPOSED PATTERN
Structure, tests, CI/CD, bundles, environment promotion and authenticated integrations aren't independent checkboxes — a fragile notebook estate needs all of them together, not whichever one is fastest to add this sprint.

## Apply it

title: T08 · Enterprise Architecture, Migration & Production Operations

lessons.title: Current & Target Architecture & Migration Strategy & Cutover
lessons.body:
## Your learning goal

Design a current-to-target enterprise architecture and operate the migration, cutover and production-readiness disciplines that get it there safely — and keep it running once it's live

## Practice case

The following organization is an illustrative training case from the supplied deck.

## A decade of undocumented sprawl, with no plan for getting out of it

Ashcombe is a large regional insurer whose data estate has grown for a decade into an undocumented sprawl: an on-prem Hadoop cluster, a Teradata warehouse, and dozens of point-to-point ETL jobs nobody has fully mapped
Workloads are being migrated to Databricks ad hoc, team by team, in whatever order seems easiest, with no defined cutover criteria and no rollback plan if a migrated workload breaks
There is no observability on the migrated workloads — the platform team finds out about a failure when a business user calls to ask why a report is stale, not from a dashboard or an alert
A regional data-center outage last year caused a multi-day scramble, because there was no tested disaster-recovery plan and no incident-response runbook — just whoever happened to be online at the time
Anyone with workspace access can push a change directly to production; there is no production-readiness gate, and no platform operating model defining who actually owns the shared estate

## A documented architecture, a gated migration, and a named owner for every workload

A documented current-state inventory mapped to a target lakehouse architecture, with every existing workload assigned exactly one destination before migration starts
Workloads migrated in prioritized, risk-ordered waves, each with defined cutover criteria and a tested rollback path — not ad hoc, team-by-team migration
A full observability stack — dashboards, alerts, SLOs — instrumented before a workload reaches production, so failures are caught by the platform, not reported by a business user
A tested disaster-recovery plan (RTO/RPO per workload tier) and a formal incident-response runbook, replacing “whoever happens to be online”
A production-readiness gate checking every workload's go-live, backed by a platform operating model that names who owns what — the central platform team's guardrails vs. each workload team's own pipelines

## An inventory first, then a target that accounts for every workload

Core ideas
A current-state assessment inventories every workload, its dependencies, and its risk — not just the ones somebody remembers to mention — before any target architecture gets drawn
A target architecture maps every current-state workload to exactly one destination in the new estate; it is not a green-field design that only accounts for the easy cases
The assessment has to cover more than compute and storage — governance, ownership and how each workload is actually used are part of the same inventory, because they shape what “done” looks like for that workload
WHY IT MATTERS
Ashcombe's undocumented Hadoop-plus-Teradata sprawl is exactly why nobody could plan a coherent migration — there was no inventory to sequence against
This is the foundation every later subtopic in this module builds on — migration strategy (03) needs a target to migrate toward, and workload migration (04) needs to know what each workload actually is
A target architecture that skips documenting the current state first isn't safer for being simpler — it's a plan that will collide with an undiscovered workload partway through migration

## Current state: point-to-point sprawl. Target state: a documented lakehouse.

CURRENT STATE: POINT-TO-POINT SPRAWL
An on-prem Hadoop cluster and a Teradata
warehouse, connected by dozens of one-off
ETL jobs nobody has fully mapped, with no
single owner for the whole estate
TARGET STATE: A DOCUMENTED LAKEHOUSE
One inventoried architecture — ingestion,
medallion layers, governance and serving —
with every current-state workload mapped to
exactly one target-state destination
before migration starts
ASSESSMENT DIMENSION
CURRENT STATE
TARGET STATE
Compute
Fixed-size Hadoop cluster, always on
Elastic, workload-scoped Databricks compute
Storage & governance
Teradata schemas plus ungoverned HDFS
One governed lakehouse under Unity Catalog
Ownership
No single team accountable for the estate
A named platform operating model (chapter 08)

## A sequenced plan, and a cutover that's earned, not scheduled

Core ideas
Migration strategy sequences workloads into prioritized waves by risk and dependency — not by whichever team happens to be ready first
Cutover is a deliberate, criteria-gated event: production traffic switches only once validation proves the new system matches the old one, not whenever migration “feels” done
A parallel-run (shadow) period — running old and new side by side and comparing output — is what actually proves equivalence before cutover, not a one-time spot-check
WHY IT MATTERS
Ashcombe's ad hoc, no-cutover-criteria migration is exactly the failure mode this subtopic exists to prevent
This turns chapter 02's mapped target architecture into an actual sequencing plan — a target diagram alone doesn't tell you what moves first
Sets up chapter 04's workload-specific migration approaches — the wave a workload belongs in, and its cutover criteria, depend on what kind of workload it is

## Assess current state → plan migration waves → migrate & validate → cutover

ASSESS CURRENT STATE
Inventory workloads,
dependencies, and risk
PLAN MIGRATION WAVES
Sequence by risk and
business dependency
MIGRATE & VALIDATE
Run old and new in
parallel, compare output
CUTOVER
Switch production traffic
once the gate is met
CUTOVER PATTERN
WHAT IT IS
WHEN IT FITS
Big bang
Every workload switches at once, on one date
Small estates, or when parallel-running isn't feasible
Phased / wave-based
Workloads cut over in prioritized, risk-ordered groups
Most enterprise migrations — Ashcombe's approach

New system runs alongside the old one before cutover

lessons.title: Workload Migration & Observability & Troubleshooting
lessons.body:
## The migration technique has to match the workload, not the other way around

Core ideas
Different workload types need different migration techniques — batch ETL, interactive BI, and ML/streaming workloads don't migrate the same way, and a single lift-and-shift approach fails at least one of them
Batch ETL should be re-architected (e.g. into Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines), not just relocated — a lift-and-shift of legacy scripts carries the legacy problems straight into the new platform
ML and streaming workloads carry the highest migration risk, because a stateful, continuously-running workload can't be validated with a single point-in-time comparison the way a batch job can
WHY IT MATTERS
Treating migration as one uniform technique across every workload type is a common and costly mistake — it under-serves the workloads that actually need a different approach
This ties directly into chapter 03's cutover criteria — the validation method that proves a workload is ready to cut over differs by workload type
Ashcombe's dozens of undocumented ETL jobs span all three categories, which is exactly why chapter 02's inventory has to capture workload type, not just workload existence

## Three signal types, each answering a different question

Core ideas
Observability has to be instrumented before a workload reaches production, not added after the first incident — metrics, logs and lineage captured as the workload runs, tied to defined SLOs
A full observability stack means more than “we have some dashboards” — job/pipeline metrics, cluster/query performance, and data lineage/freshness are three distinct signal types, each answering a different question
Troubleshooting uses evidence — the Spark UI's stage detail, system tables, the lineage graph — to isolate the actual cause, not guessing based on what changed most recently
WHY IT MATTERS
Ashcombe found out about failures from angry business users calling in — the direct, avoidable cost of skipping this subtopic entirely
This is what makes chapter 06's incident response actually fast — you can't triage or diagnose an incident using signals that don't exist
This is exactly what chapter 07's production-readiness gate checks for before a workload goes live — not whether observability could theoretically be added later

lessons.title: Disaster Recovery & Incident Response & Production Readiness
lessons.body:
## Tested, not documented — and owned before an incident, not during one

Core ideas
Disaster recovery means a defined RTO/RPO per workload tier plus a tested failover — not a plan that exists only as a document nobody has actually run
Incident response is a repeatable sequence — detect, triage, communicate, resolve, postmortem — not improvisation by whoever happens to be online when something breaks
A named on-call owner has to exist before an incident happens, not get assigned reactively once one is already underway
WHY IT MATTERS
Ashcombe's regional outage, handled with no runbook at all, is the direct, multi-day cost of skipping both halves of this subtopic
This ties directly into chapter 07's production-readiness gate, which checks that a DR tier and an on-call owner are assigned before a workload goes live — not that they exist somewhere in theory
The same observability instrumented in chapter 05 is what makes triage in an actual incident fast — you can't triage using signals that were never built

## Disaster recovery and incident response, side by side

DISASTER RECOVERY
Defined RTO/RPO per workload tier
Cross-region replication for what
actually needs it — not everything
Tested failover, not a plan on a shelf
INCIDENT RESPONSE
Detect → triage → communicate →
resolve → postmortem, every time
A named on-call owner, not "whoever
happens to see the alert first"
PATTERN
WHAT IT COVERS
EXAMPLE
RTO / RPO target
How fast a workload must recover, and how much data loss is tolerable
A tier-1 fraud pipeline: RTO 1 hour, RPO 5 minutes

Actually exercising the DR plan, not just documenting it

## Every category checked, with a named owner, before go-live

Core ideas
A production-readiness gate checks every category — observability, data quality, DR/rollback, access/governance, ownership/on-call — before a workload goes live, not after
The gate needs a named owner per category, not a single generic sign-off from one person — a checklist item with nobody accountable for it gets checked off without actually being true
Skipping the gate under deadline pressure is exactly how Ashcombe's individual gaps (no observability, no tested DR, no named owner) compounded into an outage with no clear owner to even call
WHY IT MATTERS
This is where chapters 02 through 06 actually get enforced — a target architecture, a migration plan, an observability stack and a DR plan are only real if something actually checks for them before a workload ships
The gate is what chapter 08's platform operating model is responsible for maintaining at scale, across many workload teams, not just one
A gate that exists on paper but nobody actually enforces under deadline pressure is functionally the same as having no gate at all

PRODUCTION READINESS GATE — a workload does not go live until every category below is checked off

lessons.title: Platform Operating Model & Architecture & Operations Trade-offs
lessons.body:
## Who owns what, and how a change actually gets approved

Core ideas
A platform operating model defines who owns what: a central platform team sets shared guardrails — governance, CI/CD patterns, cost, the production-readiness gate itself — while workload teams own their own pipelines within those guardrails
A shared change process defines who reviews and approves a given kind of production change, and how fast — not an ad hoc decision made differently every time
Neither fully centralized nor fully federated ownership works alone: centralized is too slow for individual teams' day-to-day work, and federated alone lets standards drift apart across teams
WHY IT MATTERS
Without a defined operating model, “who owns this” gets answered ad hoc every single time something breaks — exactly Ashcombe's gap, and exactly why the regional outage had no clear owner to call
This is what makes chapter 07's production-readiness gate actually enforceable at scale, across many workload teams, rather than depending on one person's memory or goodwill
A platform with dozens of workload teams and no operating model is how Ashcombe's original architecture — not necessarily wrong on paper — drifted into an undocumented sprawl in the first place

## Central platform team and workload teams, and how they share ownership

CENTRAL PLATFORM TEAM
Owns shared standards: governance,
CI/CD patterns, cost guardrails,
the production readiness gate itself
WORKLOAD TEAMS
Own their own pipelines end to end,
within the platform team's standards —
not a ticket queue to a central team
←→
ROLE
RESPONSIBILITY
EXAMPLE DECISION
Platform team
Sets the guardrails every workload must operate inside
Approves the standard CI/CD template every team's pipeline uses
Workload team
Builds and operates its own pipelines inside those guardrails
Decides its own migration wave order within the approved plan
Shared change process
Who reviews and approves a production change, and how fast
A schema change to a shared table requires platform-team sign-off

## A durable choice against a faster one, at every layer of this module

Core ideas
Big bang migration finishes faster and is simpler to plan, but is far riskier to reverse; phased, wave-based migration takes longer but lets each wave's problems surface — and get fixed — before the next wave starts
Active-active disaster recovery costs more to run continuously but recovers essentially instantly; active-passive costs less day to day but takes longer to fail over and depends entirely on that failover actually being tested
A production-readiness gate adds friction before every go-live, but the alternative — self-service go-live — shifts the risk onto whoever skips a step under deadline pressure, exactly as happened at Ashcombe
WHY IT MATTERS
Ashcombe's failure mode was choosing the faster, less-disciplined option every time — ad hoc migration over waves, no tested DR over an active DR posture, self-service production changes over a gate — and each individually-reasonable shortcut compounded into an outage nobody could diagnose or own
Every one of these trade-offs has a “fast/cheap now” side and a “safe and durable” side — the module's whole point is recognizing which one a given moment and workload tier actually calls for, not defaulting to one side reflexively
This is the direct rehearsal for the defend stage — candidates must be able to name a trade-off, state both sides, and say which fact tipped it for Ashcombe specifically

## Two trade-offs, always named and justified

THE TRADE-OFFS
Centralized vs. federated platform operating model — which one is actually durable once the number of workload teams grows past a handful
Gated vs. self-service production readiness — under time pressure, which one actually reduces risk rather than just moving it onto whoever is in a hurry
WHAT A STRONG DEFENSE SOUNDS LIKE
Names the specific trade-off, states both sides, and points at the fact that tips it — not just the pattern name
“We used a phased, wave-based migration because Ashcombe's workloads have deep, undocumented cross-dependencies that a big-bang cutover couldn't safely validate all at once” — not “we used phased migration because it's best practice”
Production operations maturity belongs here too — architecture, migration strategy, observability, DR, incident response, the readiness gate and the operating model are one composed pattern, not independent checkboxes to tick separately

## Two concrete decisions candidates must be able to defend

Big bang vs. phased migration
A single cutover date is faster to finish but riskier to reverse; phased waves take longer but let each wave's problems surface before the next one starts
Active-active vs. active-passive DR
Active-active costs more to run continuously but recovers instantly; active-passive is cheaper but takes longer to fail over and needs a tested plan
Centralized vs. federated operating model
Centralized platform ownership is more consistent but slower for individual teams; federated ownership moves faster but risks standards drifting apart
Gated vs. self-service production readiness
A gate catches problems before go-live but adds friction; self-service moves faster but shifts the risk onto whoever skips a step under deadline pressure
PRODUCTION OPERATIONS IS A COMPOSED PATTERN
Architecture, migration strategy, observability, DR, incident response, production readiness and the operating model aren't independent checkboxes — a workload is only actually production-ready when all of them are true at once, not whichever one is fastest to check off this sprint.

lessons.title: AI/BI Dashboards & Semantic Models
lessons.body:
## Your learning goal

Design a governed semantic layer — semantic models and metric views — that AI/BI dashboards and Genie both query, so a business question gets the same trusted answer however it's asked

## Practice case

The following organization is an illustrative training case from the supplied deck.

## Four tools, four independent guesses at the same number

Marlstone is a multi-brand consumer packaged goods company whose Finance, Merchandising and Store Operations teams each built their own “revenue per store” dashboard, directly on raw tables, with their own bespoke SQL defining the metric independently
A governance review surfaced the problem when three executive dashboards showed three different regional revenue-per-store figures for the same week, and nobody could say which one was right
Genie was deployed on top of the same raw tables with no semantic layer underneath it, so it produces a fourth independent answer whenever a business user asks about revenue per store in plain English
No metric anywhere in the business carries a visible certification — there is no single definition anyone can point to as the trusted one, only four tools that each quietly assumed they were right
Business users have started keeping their own spreadsheets to reconcile the dashboards by hand, which is exactly the opposite of what self-service analytics was supposed to replace

## One governed layer, queried consistently by every tool

A semantic model defining Marlstone's dimensions, measures and relationships once, with the trusted version of each metric visibly certified
Metric views defining calculation logic — including “revenue per store” — exactly once, so every consuming tool resolves it identically instead of copy-pasting its own version
AI/BI dashboards built on top of the semantic layer instead of raw tables, so a dashboard's numbers are inherited from the governed definition, not authored fresh per dashboard
Genie (and, where appropriate, Genie One) answering only through that same governed layer, with the reasoning behind every answer shown so it can be checked, not just trusted on faith

## Datasets, widgets and filters — inherited trust, not authored fresh

Core ideas
An AI/BI dashboard is assembled from datasets, widgets and filters — its value depends entirely on what those datasets are built against, not on how the dashboard looks
A dataset built directly against raw tables encodes its own private definition of every metric it touches; a dataset built against the semantic layer inherits the certified definition instead
A widget visualizes a dataset's output, and a filter narrows it — neither one changes what the underlying metric actually means
WHY IT MATTERS
Marlstone's three conflicting revenue-per-store dashboards all exist for the same reason: each one was built directly on raw tables, with its own bespoke SQL quietly defining “revenue” independently
This is the first subtopic specifically because every later one — semantic models, metric views, Genie — only matters if dashboards are actually built to consume them, not built to bypass them
A dashboard's trustworthiness is inherited, not authored fresh each time — chapter 03 is where that inheritance actually gets defined

## Data modeled in Unity Catalog → semantic layer defines metrics → dashboard built on top → business user self-serves

DATA MODELED IN UNITY CATALOG
Tables governed, with lineage
and permissions already in place
SEMANTIC LAYER DEFINES METRICS

dimensions sit on top

semantic layer, not raw SQL

DASHBOARD ELEMENT
WHAT IT DOES
EXAMPLE

Revenue per store, pulled from the semantic layer

A single chart, table or KPI tile on the canvas
A bar chart of revenue per store by region

A control that narrows every widget on the page at once
A quarter selector applied across the whole dashboard

## The layer between physical tables and every consuming tool

Core ideas
A semantic model sits between physical tables in Unity Catalog and every tool that consumes data — it defines dimensions, measures and relationships once, in one place
A dimension is an attribute a measure can be sliced by; a measure is a named, reusable aggregation; a relationship connects entities so a query can join them correctly without being rebuilt by hand
Certification is the visible signal that a given piece of the semantic model is the trusted, reviewed version — not just something someone happened to build
WHY IT MATTERS
Marlstone's three conflicting dashboards are a semantic-model gap specifically — there is no single model defining what “revenue” or “store” even means before any dashboard or Genie ever touches it
This is the structural foundation chapter 04's metric views build directly on top of — metric views define calculation logic, but they rely on the dimensions and relationships a semantic model already established
A certified semantic model is what makes “which definition is right” an answerable question instead of a four-way guess

## Written once, not copy-pasted per report

Core ideas
A metric view defines calculation logic exactly once — a measure, the dimensions it can be sliced by, and any time-based window comparison it needs — so it never has to be rewritten per report
A metric view builds on top of the entities a semantic model already defined — it's specifically about the calculation logic, not a replacement for the broader semantic model
Once defined, a metric view is queried consistently by any tool — a dashboard, Genie, or a raw SQL query — and every one of them gets the same number
WHY IT MATTERS
Marlstone's revenue-per-store metric is exactly this kind of calculation — defined as a metric view exactly once, it stops being something each dashboard has to reinvent
This is what chapter 02's dashboards and chapter 05's Genie both actually query against once it exists — without a metric view, both are back to guessing independently
A metric view with a defined time window (e.g. month-over-month) is what makes a comparison trustworthy — without it, two reports can silently compare different time grains and still look consistent

The choice between a scoped Genie space and enterprise-wide Genie One is itself one of chapter 09's trade-offs — it isn't a free upgrade, it's a scope decision with a governance cost

lessons.body:
## Three failure modes, and how governance catches each one

Core ideas
A natural-language question is parsed for intent, its terms are matched to certified metrics, SQL is generated against the semantic layer, and the answer returns with the query logic shown
Three failure modes recur: an ambiguous term (“sales” could mean bookings or recognized revenue), a metric that doesn't exist yet, and a wrong time grain (mixing a daily figure with a monthly one)
Governance is what catches each failure mode — a certified metric removes the ambiguity, Genie says a metric doesn't exist rather than guessing, and the metric view's defined time grain keeps a comparison valid
WHY IT MATTERS
This is where chapter 04's metric views and chapter 05's Genie mechanics actually combine into a working conversational answer — neither one alone resolves a natural-language question correctly
Marlstone's “revenue” ambiguity is resolved specifically here — because it maps to exactly one certified measure, Genie has nothing left to guess about
This is the subtopic assessors probe hardest during the defend stage — “what happens when the question doesn't map cleanly” is a stronger test of governance than a question that already works

## Four categories that make self-service trustworthy, not just fast

Core ideas
Access control governs who can see which rows or columns of a metric, typically inherited from Unity Catalog permissions rather than reimplemented per tool
Certification is a visible flag on the one approved version of a metric; lineage and audit make every dashboard and Genie answer traceable back to its source
Curation is what a space owner controls about what's discoverable and how it's explained — it's what keeps Genie One's default scope trustworthy rather than sprawling
WHY IT MATTERS
Each of these four categories maps to a concrete Marlstone control — regional managers seeing only their own region's revenue, a visible “Certified” badge on the approved metric, a Genie answer that traces back to its source tables, and only certified spaces appearing in Genie One's default scope
Governance and self-service are not opposing goals here — access control and curation are what make broad self-service safe to grant at all
This is the direct rehearsal for chapter 09's access trade-off — how broad to make self-service access without losing the trust these four categories provide

lessons.title: Business Use Cases & T09 Trade-offs
lessons.body:
## One governed layer, serving Finance, Merchandising, Store Ops and Marketing at once

Core ideas
A business question gets asked, mapped to a certified metric, and answered consistently across every function that asks a version of it — the governed layer doesn't just serve one team's use case
Finance, Merchandising, Store Operations and Marketing all draw on the same certified metrics, even though the specific question each one asks looks different on the surface
This is the payoff chapter — proof the governed semantic layer actually serves the business day to day, not just something IT built and moved on from
WHY IT MATTERS
This ties directly back to chapter 01's stat cards — “one number, not four” only matters if every function that needs that number actually gets the same one, which is exactly what this subtopic demonstrates
If self-service is too locked down, adoption suffers and business users go back to spreadsheets, exactly as Marlstone's teams already started doing; if it's too open, trust suffers instead
That tension — adoption versus trust — is exactly what chapter 09's trade-offs make explicit as a decision, not something to avoid thinking about

## Business question asked → mapped to a certified metric → answered consistently across functions

BUSINESS QUESTION ASKED
In a dashboard, or typed
straight to Genie
MAPPED TO A CERTIFIED METRIC
The same measure, wherever
the question is asked

same number, not two
BUSINESS FUNCTION
EXAMPLE QUESTION
GOVERNED METRIC USED
Finance
What was gross margin last quarter, by brand?
Certified gross_margin metric
Merchandising
Which SKUs had the steepest revenue decline this month?
revenue_mom_change measure
Store Operations
What's revenue per store, by region, this week?
revenue_per_store metric view
Marketing
Which campaigns drove the highest incremental revenue?
incremental_revenue metric

## Speed against trust, at every layer of this module

Core ideas
Broad self-service access speeds adoption but risks misuse of ungoverned raw tables; tightly governed access protects trust but can bottleneck on the platform team
Certifying a metric immediately gives users a trusted number fast but risks certifying something that later turns out wrong; iterating in draft first avoids that risk but leaves users without a trusted number in the meantime
Neither side of either trade-off is simply correct — the right call depends on the specific stakes and timeline in front of a candidate, not a fixed rule
WHY IT MATTERS
Marlstone's engagement shows what happens when these trade-offs are resolved by default rather than deliberately — no access control at all, no certification process, four tools each independently guessing
Every one of these trade-offs has a “move fast” side and a “protect trust” side — recognizing which one a given moment actually calls for is the whole point of this module
This is the direct rehearsal for the defend stage — candidates must name a trade-off, state both sides, and say which fact tipped it for Marlstone specifically

## Two more trade-offs, always named and justified

THE TRADE-OFFS
Genie scoped to one certified space vs. Genie One spanning everything
Building the semantic layer up front vs. growing it incrementally as dashboards get built
WHAT A STRONG DEFENSE SOUNDS LIKE
Names the specific trade-off, states both sides, and points at the fact that tips it — not just the pattern name
“We scoped Genie to one certified space because the certified metrics were still limited to one function, not because Genie One is somehow inferior” — not “we used a scoped space because that's best practice”
A semantic model, metric views and Genie are one composed governed layer, not three independent checkboxes to tick separately

## Two concrete decisions candidates must be able to defend

Broad self-service access vs. tightly governed access
Broad access speeds adoption but risks misuse of ungoverned raw tables; tightly governed access protects trust but can bottleneck on the platform team
Certifying a metric immediately vs. iterating in draft first
Certifying immediately gives users a trusted number fast but risks certifying something that later turns out wrong; iterating in draft avoids that risk but leaves users without a trusted number in the meantime
Genie scoped to one certified space vs. Genie One spanning everything
A scoped space guarantees every answer is governed but can frustrate a user whose question falls outside it; Genie One feels more capable but requires broader upfront certification
Building the semantic layer up front vs. growing it as dashboards get built
Building it up front avoids rework but delays the first dashboard; growing it incrementally ships value sooner but risks metrics defined inconsistently along the way
GOVERNANCE AND SELF-SERVICE ARE THE SAME DESIGN PROBLEM
A semantic model, certified metric views and Genie aren't three separate features — self-service only actually scales when every one of them resolves to the same governed definition, not three parallel paths to a different number.

## Apply it

Use the practice case to explain one decision these topics change. Name the requirement, an alternative and the trade-off. The three questions below check your understanding. Pass at least two to unlock the next lesson; you can retry.
