title: C01-C02 · Problem Framing, Discovery, Solution Design & Recommendation

lessons.title: Consulting Mindset, Root Causes & Hypotheses & Issue Trees & MECE Structuring
lessons.body:
## Your learning goal

Diagnose a client's real problem, run a structured discovery, generate and evaluate options, and turn the analysis into a clear, defensible recommendation

## Practice case

The following organization is an illustrative training case from the supplied deck.

## A symptom reported, with no diagnosis behind it

Fenwick's Head of Data has told the account team, in one sentence, that “Databricks is slow and expensive” — with no supporting detail volunteered
No structured discovery has happened yet: no stakeholder map, no current-state baseline, no agreed success measure for what “fixed” would even look like
A previous vendor proposed a single architecture change with no alternatives shown and no evaluation criteria stated — the client rejected it on instinct, not evidence
Three different Fenwick stakeholders (data engineering, finance, the airline's operations leadership) each have a different, unstated theory of what's actually wrong
The account team's instinct is to jump straight to a technical fix — exactly the shortcut this module exists to prevent

## A structured diagnosis, then a defensible recommendation

An issue tree that breaks “slow and expensive” into MECE branches — compute & configuration, query & pipeline design, governance & ways of working — before any fix is proposed
A structured discovery interview that surfaces stakeholder goals, current state, constraints, success measures and non-functional requirements, not just the one complaint volunteered
At least three options generated and scored against the same explicit criteria — risk, cost, complexity, scalability, security, operating model — not one option defended after the fact
A recommendation structured as situation-complication-question, with the answer stated up front, backed by evidence, and closed with a roadmap and a clear decision ask

## What the client says first is a symptom, not the answer

Core ideas
A consulting mindset treats the client's opening statement as a symptom to investigate, not a problem statement to solve literally — “it's slow and expensive” is a complaint, not a diagnosis
A hypothesis is a specific, testable explanation for the symptom — not a hunch stated as fact and not a shortcut to skip discovery
Business impact has to be named early: what does this symptom actually cost the client, in terms they care about, not just in technical terms
WHY IT MATTERS
Fenwick's account team jumping straight to a technical fix is exactly the mistake this subtopic exists to prevent — a fix for the wrong root cause fails, and looks like consulting malpractice
This is the foundation every later subtopic builds on — chapter 03's issue tree organizes the hypotheses this subtopic generates, and chapter 06's options only make sense once a root cause is confirmed
A named business impact is what makes a diagnosis land with a non-technical stakeholder, not just a technical one

## Symptom reported → hypotheses generated → tested against evidence → root cause isolated

SYMPTOM REPORTED
What the client actually
said — a complaint, not a diagnosis
HYPOTHESES GENERATED
Several plausible root
causes, named explicitly
TESTED AGAINST EVIDENCE
Each hypothesis checked
against data, not assumed
ROOT CAUSE ISOLATED
The specific, confirmed
cause a fix can target
SYMPTOM
A LIKELY (UNTESTED) HYPOTHESIS
HOW YOU'D TEST IT
“Dashboards are slow”
Query design, not cluster size, is the bottleneck
Compare query plans before assuming compute is undersized
“Databricks costs too much”
Idle clusters are running, not that usage itself is too high
Pull cluster utilization data before proposing a cheaper tier
“Reports are often wrong”
A governance/ownership gap, not a tooling defect
Trace one wrong report back to its source table and owner

## Branches that don't overlap, and don't leave anything out

Core ideas
An issue tree breaks a broad symptom into branches, each a distinct category of possible cause — not a random list of ideas
MECE means the branches are Mutually Exclusive (no overlap between them) and Collectively Exhaustive (nothing plausible is left out) — both properties have to hold, not just one
Each branch should be specific enough to generate its own testable sub-hypotheses, not so broad it can't actually be investigated
WHY IT MATTERS
Without MECE structuring, two branches can silently investigate the same thing twice while a third real cause goes unexamined entirely
This turns chapter 02's individual hypotheses into an organized, presentable structure — the tree is what a candidate can actually show a client, not just a list in their head
This is the direct rehearsal for chapter 06's option generation — options should map back to which branch of the tree they actually address

## Why is Databricks slow and expensive? — a MECE issue tree

WHY IS DATABRICKS SLOW AND EXPENSIVE?
COMPUTE & CONFIGURATION
Cluster sizing, autoscaling,
idle time, instance types
QUERY & PIPELINE DESIGN
Join strategy, partitioning,
file layout, repeated scans
GOVERNANCE & WAYS OF WORKING
Ownership, workspace sprawl,
no cost or usage review cadence
BRANCH
MECE CHECK
EXAMPLE SUB-HYPOTHESIS
Compute & configuration
Distinct from query design — a sizing problem, not a logic problem
Clusters are over-provisioned for actual peak load
Query & pipeline design
Distinct from compute — a logic problem, not a sizing problem
A daily job re-scans the full table instead of only new data
Governance & ways of working
Distinct from both — a process problem, not a technical one
No one reviews or decommissions unused clusters and jobs

## Apply it

questions.explanation: a consulting mindset treats the opening statement as a symptom to investigate, not a settled diagnosis to act on literally.

options.label: It's whatever the client already believes

options.label: Branches should be ranked by likelihood

lessons.title: Discovery: Questioning, Listening & Stakeholder Goals & Current State, Constraints, Success Measures & NFRs
lessons.body:
## Open first, clarify second, confirm last

Core ideas
Open questions surface the full shape of a problem before narrowing in — asking a yes/no question first forecloses whatever the client hadn't thought to mention
Active listening means reflecting back what's heard and leaving room for silence, not filling every pause with the next scripted question
Every stakeholder in a discovery interview has their own goal, and those goals can conflict — surfacing the conflict is part of discovery, not something to paper over
WHY IT MATTERS
Fenwick's one-sentence complaint is exactly what a discovery interview exists to expand — the “real” problem is usually broader and more specific than the opening statement
This is what generates the evidence chapter 02's hypotheses need to actually be tested — discovery isn't separate from diagnosis, it's how the diagnosis gets confirmed
Unsurfaced stakeholder goal conflicts resurface later, usually during the recommendation — better to find them in discovery than in the steering committee

## Open questions → active listening → stakeholder goals mapped → requirements captured

OPEN QUESTIONS
Surface the full picture
before narrowing in
ACTIVE LISTENING
Reflect back what's heard;
let silence draw out more
STAKEHOLDER GOALS MAPPED
Whose success looks like
what, and by when
REQUIREMENTS CAPTURED
Current state, constraints
and success measures written down
QUESTION TYPE
WHAT IT SURFACES
EXAMPLE
Open
The full shape of the problem, not a pre-narrowed answer
“Walk me through what happens when a dashboard is slow”
Clarifying
What a vague complaint actually means, specifically
“When you say expensive — compared to what budget or baseline?”
Confirming
Whether what was heard is actually what was meant
“So the real cost concern is unpredictability, not the total spend?”

## Four distinct categories, each captured explicitly

Core ideas
Current state is what actually exists today — architecture, process, cost — documented, not assumed from the client's description alone
Constraints are what genuinely can't change (budget, timeline, skills) — distinct from things that are just assumed fixed but could actually flex
Success measures are the specific, agreed way “fixed” will be judged, and non-functional requirements are the performance, security and reliability targets stated explicitly, not left implicit
WHY IT MATTERS
Without a documented current state, a recommendation can't be shown to actually improve on what exists — there's no baseline to compare against
An unstated success measure means the client and the consultant can walk away from the engagement with different definitions of whether it worked
This is the requirement map chapter 06's options get evaluated against — skipping this subtopic means chapter 07's evaluation criteria have nothing concrete to check against

## Four categories, each captured in the requirement map

CURRENT STATE
What exists today —
architecture, process, cost
CONSTRAINTS
Budget, timeline, skills,
what can't change
SUCCESS MEASURES
How “fixed” will actually
be judged, by whom
NON-FUNCTIONAL REQS
Performance, security,
reliability targets
CATEGORY
WHAT IT CAPTURES
EXAMPLE FROM FENWICK
Current state
The architecture and process as they actually work today
Three clusters running 24/7 regardless of actual query load
Constraints
What genuinely can't change, versus what's just assumed fixed
A board-approved budget ceiling, not to be exceeded mid-year
Success measures
The specific, agreed way “fixed” will be judged
Dashboard load time under 5 seconds, cost down 20% by Q3
Non-functional reqs
Performance, security and reliability targets, stated explicitly
99.9% uptime for the booking dashboard during peak travel season

questions.explanation: a narrow question asked early forecloses whatever the client hadn't thought to volunteer; open questions surface the full picture first.

options.label: It doesn't matter as long as the recommendation sounds reasonable

A constraint genuinely can't move; an assumption is untested and might actually be flexible

lessons.title: Generating Options & Evaluation Criteria & Trade-off Analysis
lessons.body:
## Real alternatives first, then a shared scorecard

Core ideas
Generating options means proposing genuinely different approaches — not one preferred solution plus two strawmen designed to lose
Evaluation criteria have to be explicit and applied the same way to every option — criteria invented after an option is already favored are not evaluation, they're justification
An option matrix makes the comparison visible and checkable by someone who wasn't in the room, not just a conclusion asserted at the end
WHY IT MATTERS
Fenwick already rejected one prior recommendation that showed no alternatives — a single option with no comparison reads as an assertion, not an analysis
This is where chapter 03's issue tree and chapter 05's requirement map actually get used — options should map back to a confirmed root cause and be checked against the captured constraints
Sets up chapter 07's deeper trade-off analysis — the option matrix is the first pass; chapter 07 goes deeper on each criterion

## Three options, scored against the same criteria

OPTION A — OPTIMIZE CURRENT SETUP
Right-size clusters, fix
query patterns, no platform change
OPTION B — RE-ARCHITECT ON DATABRICKS
Redesign the pipeline and
governance model, same platform
OPTION C — MIGRATE ELSEWHERE
Move off Databricks
entirely to a different platform
CRITERION
OPTION A
OPTION B
OPTION C
Cost to implement
Low
Medium
High
Risk
Low
Medium
High
Time to value
Fast
Moderate
Slow
Solves the root cause
Partially
Fully
Fully, at high cost

## Six criteria, applied consistently, with the trade-off named out loud

Core ideas
Risk, cost, complexity, scalability, security and operating model are six distinct dimensions — a strong option on one dimension can be weak on another, and both have to be shown
Cost means total cost, not just the upfront sticker price of implementation — ongoing run cost is part of the same evaluation
Operating model — who runs this day to day, and whether they're resourced for it — is as real a trade-off dimension as the more obviously technical ones, and it's the one most often left out
WHY IT MATTERS
A trade-off analysis that only scores the recommended option honestly, and hand-waves the others, is indistinguishable from having only ever considered one option
This is what chapter 08's recommendation actually has to defend — “why this option” only holds up if the trade-offs against the alternatives were genuinely worked through, not asserted
The operating-model dimension specifically is what chapter 09's capstone trade-offs chapter returns to — it's the dimension most often skipped under deadline pressure

## Six criteria, applied the same way to every option

SIX CRITERIA, APPLIED THE SAME WAY TO EVERY OPTION
CRITERION
WHAT IT MEASURES
RED FLAG TO WATCH FOR

How likely the option is to fail, and how bad that failure would be

Operating model

lessons.title: Structuring the Recommendation & Framing & Recommendation Trade-offs
lessons.body:
## The answer first, then the evidence that earns it

Core ideas
Situation-Complication-Question frames the context so the reader arrives at the same question the recommendation is about to answer — it's not scene-setting for its own sake
The recommendation is stated up front, not built up to — a senior, time-pressed audience needs the answer before the supporting detail
Evidence, a roadmap and explicit next steps are what turn a recommendation into something a steering committee can actually act on, not just agree with in principle
WHY IT MATTERS
This is the exact structure chapter 17's real-world assessment is scored against — a five-slide recommendation that doesn't lead with the answer loses credit regardless of the quality of the underlying analysis
Fenwick's steering committee has limited time — a recommendation that takes ten minutes to get to the point risks losing the room before the ask is even made
The roadmap and next steps are what make a “yes” actionable immediately, rather than requiring a second meeting just to figure out what happens next

## SCQ → recommendation stated up front → evidence → roadmap & next steps

SITUATION → COMPLICATION → QUESTION
Frame the context and
the decision that follows
RECOMMENDATION STATED UP FRONT
The answer first, not
buried after the analysis
EVIDENCE SUPPORTING IT
The data and trade-offs
that justify the answer
ROADMAP & NEXT STEPS
What happens after the
client says yes
COMPONENT
PURPOSE
EXAMPLE LINE
Situation-Complication-Question
Gets the reader to the same question you're about to answer
“Given rising cost and flat headcount, how should Fenwick scale?”
Recommendation
States the answer before the supporting detail, not after it
“We recommend Option B: re-architect on Databricks.”
Evidence
The specific data and trade-offs that justify the recommendation
Query-plan comparison, cluster utilization, and the option matrix
Roadmap & next steps
What happens immediately after a yes, with owners and dates
Phase 1 kickoff within two weeks, named workstream owners

## A durable choice against a faster one, at every layer of this module

Core ideas
Broad discovery surfaces more but takes longer and risks scope creep; a narrow, hypothesis-led diagnosis is faster but can miss a root cause outside the initial hypotheses
Presenting one option is decisive but invites “what about X?” unless alternatives were genuinely considered; presenting several is more defensible but can look like indecision without a clear resolving ask
Leading with the answer (SCQ) respects a senior audience's time; building up to it chronologically can feel more “proven” but loses a time-pressed steering committee
WHY IT MATTERS
Fenwick's rejected prior recommendation shows what happens when these trade-offs are resolved by default rather than deliberately — one option, no visible criteria, no structured ask
Every one of these trade-offs has a “fast now” side and a “durable/defensible” side — the module's whole point is recognizing which one a given moment and client actually calls for, not defaulting to one side reflexively
This is the direct rehearsal for the defend stage — candidates must be able to name a trade-off, state both sides, and say which fact tipped it for Fenwick specifically

## Two trade-offs, always named and justified

THE TRADE-OFFS
Quantified evidence vs. qualitative judgment — which one is actually available, and which one is being dressed up as the other
How many options to formally present — enough to be defensible, not so many the ask gets lost
WHAT A STRONG DEFENSE SOUNDS LIKE
Names the specific trade-off, states both sides, and points at the fact that tips it — not just the pattern name
“We led with the recommendation because the steering committee has fifteen minutes and conflicting priorities to resolve” — not “we led with it because that's best practice”
Recommendation quality belongs here too — diagnosis, discovery, options, trade-offs and structure are one composed pattern, not independent checkboxes to tick separately

## Two concrete decisions candidates must be able to defend

Broad discovery vs. a fast, narrow diagnosis
A wide discovery surfaces more, but takes longer and risks scope creep; a narrow, hypothesis-led diagnosis is faster but can miss a root cause outside the initial hypotheses
Presenting one option vs. several
A single recommendation is decisive but invites “what about X?” unless alternatives were genuinely considered; several options are more defensible but can look like indecision if not resolved with a clear ask
Leading with the answer vs. building up to it
Leading with the recommendation (SCQ) respects a senior audience's time; building up chronologically can feel more “proven” but loses a time-pressed steering committee
Quantified evidence vs. qualitative judgment
Quantified evidence is harder to argue with but isn't always available; qualitative judgment moves faster but must be named as judgment, not dressed up as data
A RECOMMENDATION IS A COMPOSED PATTERN
Diagnosis, discovery, options, trade-offs and a structured recommendation aren't independent checkboxes — a recommendation only actually holds up under challenge when every one of them was done, not whichever step felt fastest to skip under deadline pressure.

## Apply it

title: C03-C04 · Objection Handling, Difficult Client Situations & Engagement Execution

lessons.title: Clarifying & Acknowledging the Objection & Testing Assumptions Against Evidence
lessons.body:
## Your learning goal

Handle objections and difficult client moments without losing trust, then keep the engagement itself visibly under control between meetings — actions owned, risks tracked, decisions logged

## Practice case

The following organization is an illustrative training case from the supplied deck.

## Trust eroding from two directions at once

Larkspur's COO pushed back hard in a steering meeting on a proposed reporting-cadence redesign, and the consultant on the call got defensive instead of clarifying what was actually being objected to
No RAID log has been kept for this engagement — risks and open assumptions exist only in individual team members' heads, not anywhere the client can see
Three action items from the last two meetings were never closed, and nobody on the team can say who actually owns them
A governance-model change was quietly absorbed into scope weeks ago with no record of the decision, and the COO only just found out
The COO's trust in the team is visibly eroding, and the account team doesn't yet understand why it feels worse than one bad meeting

## A deliberate response to friction, and a visibly-controlled engagement

Clarify what's actually being objected to before responding, acknowledge it as reasonable, then test the assumption behind it against evidence — not defend the original recommendation on assertion
Disagree on the merits when the evidence supports it, and escalate only if the disagreement is still unresolved after the evidence has been offered
A RAID log capturing risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies, kept current and visible to the client — not reconstructed from memory when something goes wrong
A decision log recording what was decided, by whom and why, plus a follow-up cadence that closes every action instead of letting it go quiet

## Clarify first, acknowledge second — before any response to the substance

Core ideas
An objection is rarely as specific as it sounds on first hearing — clarifying what's actually being objected to is the first move, not the last
Acknowledging validates the concern as reasonable without agreeing the underlying recommendation is wrong — the two are separate acts, not one
Responding before clarifying risks answering a different objection than the one actually being raised
WHY IT MATTERS
Larkspur's COO's objection was met with defensiveness instead of a clarifying question, which is exactly the mistake this subtopic exists to prevent
This is the entry point into the whole subtopic sequence — chapter 03's evidence-testing only works once the actual assumption behind the objection is understood, not assumed
An acknowledgment that doesn't concede ground unnecessarily is what keeps a defend-stage answer (chapter 16) credible later

## Objection raised → clarify → acknowledge → ready to respond

OBJECTION RAISED
The client pushes back — in
words, tone, or body language
CLARIFY
An open question surfaces
what's actually being objected to
ACKNOWLEDGE
The concern is validated as
reasonable, not conceded to
READY TO RESPOND
The real objection is named,
not just the loudest words
OBJECTION TYPE
CLARIFYING QUESTION
ACKNOWLEDGMENT LINE
Past vendor failed to deliver
What specifically didn't get delivered last time?
That's a fair thing to be cautious about, given what happened
Timeline feels too aggressive
Which part of the timeline concerns you most?
You're right to want to see the sequencing before committing
Cost seems higher than expected
Higher than what comparison point?
It's reasonable to want that math laid out clearly

## Test the assumption, don't just defend or concede it

Core ideas
Every objection rests on an assumption, stated or not — testing that assumption against evidence is what separates a grounded response from a guess
Evidence can confirm the assumption (the objection was right) or revise it (the objection was based on incomplete information) — both are legitimate outcomes of the test
A response grounded in fact is defensible under further challenge; a response grounded in assertion alone is not
WHY IT MATTERS
This is where chapter 02's clarified objection actually gets resolved — clarifying without testing just produces a well-understood but still-unanswered objection
Larkspur's engagement needs this discipline specifically because the previous response defended the recommendation without ever checking whether the COO's concern had merit
Sets up chapter 04 — a disagreement stated on the merits requires the evidence this subtopic produces

## Assumption surfaced → tested against evidence → confirmed or revised → response grounded in fact

ASSUMPTION SURFACED
What the objection is actually
resting on, stated explicitly
TESTED AGAINST EVIDENCE
Checked against data or the
engagement record, not memory
CONFIRMED OR REVISED
The assumption holds, or it
doesn't — both are useful
RESPONSE GROUNDED IN FACT
Answered with evidence,
not reassurance alone
ASSUMPTION
TEST
OUTCOME
This migration will fail like the last vendor's did
Compare this proposal's diagnosis and options to the failed one
A different root cause was diagnosed and options were scored — named explicitly
The timeline doesn't account for the compliance review
Check the roadmap against the review's actual lead time
The lead time was already built in — walk through the dates
The cost estimate excludes ongoing operation
Pull the total-cost figure from the trade-off analysis
Operating cost was included — show the specific line item

## Apply it

Concede immediately to avoid needing to test anything

questions.explanation: surface the assumption explicitly, test it against evidence, then let the result determine the response, rather than deciding the response first.

lessons.title: Disagreeing Without Friction & Escalation & RAID Thinking
lessons.body:
## State the disagreement on the merits, then escalate only if it's still unresolved

Core ideas
Disagreeing without friction means stating the disagreement on the merits — what the evidence actually shows — not defending a position personally or dismissing the client's concern
Escalation is a deliberate, later step for when the disagreement is still unresolved after evidence has been offered — not a first response, and not something to avoid indefinitely either
A clear signal (a repeated objection, a stalled decision, a compliance-relevant concern) is what actually triggers escalation, not discomfort alone
WHY IT MATTERS
This is the direct continuation of chapters 02-03 — clarify, acknowledge, test, and only then, if still unresolved, disagree and potentially escalate
Larkspur's team avoided disagreement entirely by getting defensive instead, which is the opposite failure mode from escalating too early — both erode trust
Escalating appropriately, with the right person, at the right signal, is what chapter 16's defend stage expects candidates to justify with specifics

## State the disagreement on the merits → offer the evidence → escalate if still unresolved

STATE THE DISAGREEMENT ON THE MERITS
Name where the evidence leads,
without softening it into agreement
OFFER THE EVIDENCE, NOT JUST AN OPINION
Point back to the specific data
or discovery finding
ESCALATE IF STILL UNRESOLVED
Bring in a second reviewer or
sponsor before trust erodes further
SIGNAL
WHY IT'S AN ESCALATION TRIGGER
WHO TO BRING IN
Same objection raised a third time
Repetition after evidence means the real concern hasn't been named yet
Engagement lead or account owner
Objection challenges the engagement's integrity, not just the recommendation
This is a trust issue, not a technical disagreement
A sponsor-level relationship owner
Stakeholder disengages rather than argues
Silence after real disagreement is a bigger risk than pushback
Whoever has the standing relationship with that stakeholder

## Four distinct categories, each captured explicitly

Core ideas
RAID stands for Risks, Assumptions, Issues and Dependencies — four distinct categories, each capturing a different kind of thing that can derail an engagement
A risk is something that might happen; an issue is something that already has; an assumption is something being treated as true but not yet confirmed; a dependency is something the engagement's progress relies on from outside the team's control
A RAID log only has value if it's kept current and visible to the client, not maintained privately and shown only when something goes wrong
WHY IT MATTERS
Larkspur's engagement had no RAID log at all — risks and open assumptions existed only in individual team members' heads, which is exactly why the COO's trust eroded when one of them surfaced as a problem
This is the structural foundation for chapter 06's decision log and chapter 08's scope decisions — both draw directly on what the RAID log has already captured
A current RAID log is itself evidence of the “clear ownership, risks, decisions and next steps” this module's engagement-execution exit standard requires

## Four categories, each captured explicitly in the RAID log

RISKS
Might happen, would hurt if
it did — tracked before it does
ASSUMPTIONS
Believed true but not yet
confirmed — tested, not ignored
ISSUES
Already happening, needs
an owner and a resolution
DEPENDENCIES
Needs something outside
the team's own control
CATEGORY
WHAT IT CAPTURES
EXAMPLE FROM LARKSPUR
Risks
What could go wrong, and how bad it would be if it did
Compliance review could delay go-live by a full sprint
Assumptions
What's believed true but hasn't been confirmed
Assuming the client's data team can support parallel testing
Issues
What's already gone wrong and needs an owner
The staging-environment access request has been pending two weeks
Dependencies
What the engagement needs from outside the team's control
Sign-off from the client's security team before cutover

options.label: Concede first, then quietly raise concerns internally

options.label: There is no meaningful difference — both are logged the same way

lessons.title: Actions, Decisions & the Decision Log & Follow-Ups & Stakeholder Cadence
lessons.body:
## Captured live, with an owner, not reconstructed from memory

Core ideas
Every meeting that produces a decision should produce a decision-log entry at the same time — captured live, not reconstructed afterward from memory
A decision-log entry needs an owner assigned, not just a decision recorded — an unassigned decision is an action nobody will actually carry out
Meeting outcomes (what was decided, why, and by whom) are distinct from meeting notes (what was discussed) — the log captures the former specifically
WHY IT MATTERS
Three of Larkspur's action items were never closed because no decision log existed to assign and track ownership in the first place — this is the exact gap this subtopic closes
This is what chapter 07's follow-up cadence actually tracks against — a follow-up without a logged decision and owner has nothing concrete to check in on
A defensible decision log, produced live, is direct evidence toward this module's engagement-execution exit standard

## Meeting happens → decisions captured → owners assigned → log updated

MEETING HAPPENS
Steering committee, working
session, or client check-in
DECISIONS CAPTURED
What was decided, written
down in the room, not after
OWNERS ASSIGNED
Every decision and action
has exactly one named owner
LOG UPDATED
The decision log reflects it
before anyone leaves
MEETING TYPE
WHAT GETS LOGGED
WHY IT MATTERS
Steering committee
Every decision made, who made it, and the date
Prevents “I don't remember agreeing to that” months later
Working session
Open questions and who owns answering them
Keeps a small decision from silently becoming an assumption
Client check-in
Any scope or priority signal, even if informal
An early signal caught here avoids a bigger change-control fight later

## Different stakeholders, different cadences — nothing closes silently

Core ideas
A logged action needs an owner who's actually been notified, not just a name attached to a row in a log
A follow-up cadence is a set interval at which an action's status gets checked — different stakeholder types warrant different cadences, not one blanket schedule
An action closes in one of two ways: it gets done, or it gets escalated — it should never simply go quiet
WHY IT MATTERS
Larkspur's three unclosed actions went quiet specifically because no cadence existed to catch them before they became a trust problem — the decision log from chapter 06 alone wasn't enough without this
This is where stakeholder cadence lives specifically — an internal sync, a client check-in and an executive touchpoint are three different cadences for three different audiences
This is direct, checkable evidence of “clear ownership... and next steps” — this module's own engagement-execution exit standard

## Action logged → owner notified → cadence check-in → closed or escalated

ACTION LOGGED
Captured with a named
owner and a date
OWNER NOTIFIED
The person responsible knows
they're responsible — explicitly
CADENCE CHECK-IN
Status confirmed at a set
interval, not left to chance
CLOSED OR ESCALATED
Done and confirmed, or flagged
before it becomes a surprise
CADENCE TYPE
FREQUENCY
PURPOSE
Internal team sync
Weekly
Catch a stalled action before the client notices
Client status check-in
Bi-weekly
Confirm outstanding actions are still on track from the client's side
Executive sponsor touchpoint
Monthly
Keep the relationship warm above the working level, independent of any open issue

lessons.title: Scope & Change Awareness & C03-C04 Trade-offs
lessons.body:
## A deliberate call, made on purpose, recorded either way

Core ideas
A change request first gets assessed against the agreed scope, not reflexively accepted or reflexively resisted
Absorbing a small change quietly keeps momentum, but sets a precedent — it should be a deliberate call, not the path of least resistance
Formal change-control protects the engagement's scope and cost baseline but can feel bureaucratic if reached for over something genuinely trivial
WHY IT MATTERS
This is the RAID log (chapter 05) in active use — a change request that gets absorbed or change-controlled should generate a RAID log update either way, not disappear into a decision nobody can trace later
Larkspur's engagement never had this decision made explicitly for any change — everything either got quietly absorbed or ignored, with no record of which
This is the direct rehearsal for the capstone trade-off in chapter 09 — absorbing vs. formal change-control is one of the trade-offs candidates must be able to name and justify

## Change request surfaces → impact assessed against scope → absorb or change-control → RAID log updated

CHANGE REQUEST SURFACES
A new ask, a moved deadline,
or a shifted definition of done
IMPACT ASSESSED AGAINST SCOPE
Checked against what was
actually agreed, not assumed
ABSORB OR CHANGE-CONTROL
A deliberate call, not a
default to whichever is easiest
RAID LOG UPDATED
The decision and its reasoning
are on record, not just in memory
SIGNAL
ABSORB QUIETLY IF…
FORMALLY CHANGE-CONTROL IF…
A new stakeholder request
It fits inside the agreed scope and takes no extra time
It adds new deliverables, timeline, or cost
A compliance deadline moves
The existing plan already accounts for it
It compresses a timeline the team already committed to
A requirement's definition shifts
It's a clarification of something already agreed
It changes what “done” actually means

## A durable choice against a faster one, at every layer of this module

Core ideas
Acknowledging a concern is not the same as conceding the underlying recommendation is wrong — acknowledging too little reads as dismissive, conceding too early abandons a defensible position under pressure alone
Absorbing a change keeps momentum but sets a precedent; formal change-control protects the baseline but can feel bureaucratic over something genuinely trivial
Resolving a disagreement yourself keeps the relationship close but risks being under-supported on a genuinely hard call; escalating brings the right authority in but can look like an inability to handle it
WHY IT MATTERS
Larkspur's engagement shows what happens when these trade-offs are resolved by default rather than deliberately — defensiveness instead of acknowledgment, no scope decision at all, no record of anything decided
Every one of these trade-offs has a “keep it moving now” side and a “protect the relationship or scope” side — recognizing which one a given moment actually calls for is the whole point of this module
This is the direct rehearsal for the defend stage — candidates must name a trade-off, state both sides, and say which fact tipped it for Larkspur specifically

## Two more trade-offs, always named and justified

THE TRADE-OFFS
A formal, written decision log vs. relying on informal memory of what was agreed
How quickly to escalate a disagreement vs. how long to keep working it at the working level
WHAT A STRONG DEFENSE SOUNDS LIKE
Names the specific trade-off, states both sides, and points at the fact that tips it — not just the pattern name
“We escalated because the objection had already been raised twice with evidence offered both times, not because the first conversation felt uncomfortable” — not “we escalated because that's best practice”
Trust, RAID discipline, decision logging and follow-up cadence are one composed pattern, not independent checkboxes to tick separately

## Two concrete decisions candidates must be able to defend

Acknowledging vs. conceding
Acknowledging validates the concern as reasonable without agreeing the recommendation is wrong; conceding too early abandons a defensible position under pressure alone
Absorbing a change vs. formal change-control
Absorbing a small change keeps momentum but sets a precedent; formal change-control protects scope but can feel bureaucratic if used for something trivial
Escalating vs. resolving it yourself
Resolving it yourself keeps the relationship close but risks being under-supported on a genuinely hard call; escalating brings the right authority in but can look like you couldn't handle it
Formal decision log vs. informal memory
A formal log is defensible months later but takes discipline to maintain; relying on memory is faster in the moment but is exactly what erodes trust when a decision is later disputed
TRUST IS A COMPOSED PATTERN
Clarifying, acknowledging, testing and evidence-based responses aren't independent techniques — trust only actually holds up under a real objection when every one of them was done, and the RAID/decision-log/cadence discipline is what keeps that trust intact between meetings too, not just during them.

## Apply it

Use the practice case to explain one decision these topics change. Name the requirement, an alternative and the trade-off. The three questions below check your understanding. Pass at least two to unlock the next lesson; you can retry.

Source: C03-C04-Objection-Handling-Engagement-Execution.pptx, slides 33–41. Adapted for self-paced reading. Live demonstrations, hidden scenario facts and independent assessment material remain outside this course.
